Article Title: 'Crime over decades': Judge unseals heavily redacted records on Ilhan Omar's home search. Did her father misrepresent her birth year so that she could become US citizen as a minor?
Article Text:
A judge released the heavily redacted documents pertaining to the raid on Congresswoman Ilhan Omar.

Why did federal agents search Ilhan Omar's home?

What is the immigration fraud investigation about?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A federal investigation into Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar has been examining alleged crimes dating back to 1980, according to newly unsealed court documents that shed light on the search of her Washington, DC, home last month. The heavily redacted records, released Monday by a federal judge, indicate that investigators are pursuing a pre-indictment case involving Omar and possible immigration fraud. However, the documents do not specify the alleged offences or disclose whether prosecutors are preparing particular criminal charges against her.One of the government filings stated: "The United States believes ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades — beginning long before she was ever in Congress." The filing also said that the investigation has nothing to do with her professional life.The records were made public following a lawsuit by more than a dozen news organisations seeking access to documents related to the federal search of Omar's residence. The 169-page collection contains extensive redactions, and a 67-page affidavit supporting the search warrant remains sealed.\Federal authorities applied for a search warrant on October 2, seeking permission to search Omar's Washington, DC, residence for documents and other evidence relating to alleged violations involving the Congresswoman.A judge approved the warrant on October 9, and Homeland Security Investigations agents executed it on October 12.The warrant authorized agents to seize papers, records, photographs, documents, physical objects, thumb drives, external hard drives, computers and cellphones registered to or used by Omar. Omar said that agents took 17 items from her home, including several cellphones, notebooks, computers and her passport. The seized items reportedly also included a children's book and a vintage camera belonging to her husband, political consultant Tim Mynett.The search warrant referred to Omar by the names "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar" and sought evidence of alleged violations dating from 1980 to the present. Three days before the raid, a judge had ordered the warrant sealed, citing concerns that public disclosure could lead to flight from prosecution, destruction or tampering with evidence, intimidation of potential witnesses and serious jeopardy to the investigation.Federal authorities are examining possible immigration fraud involving Omar or members of her family who fled war-torn Somalia in the 1990s. They are probing whether Omar's birthday was listed as October 4, 1982, rather than a year earlier, so that she became eligible for US citizenship as a minor when her father naturalized in 2000. Another focus is her 2009 marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, a British national whom investigators reportedly suspect could be her brother. The two remained legally married until 2017.Omar has repeatedly denied knowingly marrying her brother. Asked about the allegation during an October 21 interview on MS NOW's 'All In with Chris Hayes', she said: "Not to my knowledge."Investigators have revisited records relating to the marriage because Omar reportedly filed joint tax returns with her first husband, Ahmed Hirsi, at least twice during the period she was legally married to Elmi.Elmi has described himself as gay and is a PhD researcher at the University of Bristol, where his work includes research on queer violence in Kenya.The investigation is also reportedly examining the immigration paperwork of some of Omar's relatives. The Wall Street Journal previously reported that authorities had issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to family members, seeking testimony before a Minnesota grand jury.Omar, 44, immigrated to the US from Somalia in 1995 and became a naturalized citizen in 2000. She has not been charged with a crime and has denied the allegations.
Article Summary: Newly unsealed court documents shed light on the search of her Washington, DC, home last month. Records indicate that investigators are pursuing a pre- indictment case involving Omar and possible immigration fraud. Documents do not specify the alleged offences or disclose whether prosecutors are preparing particular criminal charges against her.

Article Title: Bay Area homeowners replacing broken gas furnaces from 2029 may face about $12,500 in additional costs under new emissions rules, with a new analysis finding electric heat-pump installations substanti
Article Text:
Heat pumps could significantly increase upfront expenses

Electrical upgrades remain a concern

Homeowners could save on energy bills

Changes to the regulation are still possible

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Homeowners across California’s Bay Area could face a significantly higher bill when replacing their natural gas heating systems under an upcoming emissions regulation. A new assessment by the Bay Area Air Quality Management District, reported by the San Francisco Chronicle and detailed in the district’s November 2026 implementation report, estimates that switching from a conventional gas furnace to an electric heat-pump system could add approximately $12,526 to installation costs for a typical single-family home. The requirement is part of Regulation 9, Rule 4, which aims to eliminate nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions from newly installed natural gas-fired furnaces. The pollutant contributes to ground-level ozone and particulate pollution, both of which can affect public health and regional air quality. Under the current timeline, the zero-emissions standard will apply to covered furnaces from January 1, 2029. The regulation does not require homeowners to remove existing operational gas furnaces. Instead, it restricts the sale and installation of newly manufactured gas-fired equipment that does not meet the emissions standard, meaning households replacing their systems after the deadline will need to consider compliant alternatives.The district’s cost assessment highlights the financial difference between conventional heating systems and electric alternatives. Installing a standard natural gas furnace in a single-family home is estimated to cost approximately $8,064, compared with around $20,590 for an electric heat-pump heating and cooling system.This creates an estimated upfront difference of $12,526. However, the financial comparison changes when homeowners also factor in air-conditioning expenses. Since heat pumps provide both heating and cooling, households that would otherwise purchase a separate central air-conditioning system could see the additional cost fall to approximately $2,095. The distinction is particularly relevant in the Bay Area, where an estimated 60% of homes already have central air conditioning. Existing electrical infrastructure and available space for outdoor equipment could also make certain installations less expensive.While heat pumps are expected to offer long-term savings on energy bills, the initial installation could become more complicated for properties requiring electrical upgrades. According to the Air District’s assessment, electrical panel and service upgrades can cost several thousand dollars and, in particularly difficult cases, exceed $20,000. Around 3% of single-family homes and 10% of multifamily properties in California are estimated to have electrical panels that may require upgrades for full electrification.Infrastructure limitations could also affect installation timelines. Data cited in the report indicate that utility service upgrades can take more than 300 days for single-family homes and over 500 days for multifamily buildings. The transition could create additional challenges for apartment owners and tenants, particularly in older buildings where electrical capacity is limited. The district has also identified the possibility of landlords passing some improvement expenses on to renters.Despite the higher upfront investment, electric heat pumps could reduce household energy expenses over time. A study covering three Bay Area climate zones found that households installing minimum-efficiency heat pumps could save between $167 and $474 in their first year. More efficient variable-capacity systems could generate annual savings of approximately $364 to $733, depending on the property and existing equipment.However, the actual savings will vary according to electricity rates, household energy consumption and whether a property already has air conditioning. The availability of financial assistance is another consideration. The Air District’s November assessment noted that federal incentives for residential heat pumps have declined, while state rebates through the TECH Clean California programme were fully subscribed as of September 2026. Several local programmes continue to offer incentives generally ranging from $1,000 to $3,000.The 2029 deadline is not entirely settled. The Bay Area Air District has been examining implementation challenges through a working group involving more than 40 stakeholders, including housing representatives, technical experts, manufacturers and government agencies. District staff are scheduled to present their findings to the Board of Directors on December 2, 2026.Potential changes could address properties requiring extensive electrical work, buildings without existing air-conditioning systems and situations where installation costs are particularly difficult to manage. The furnace regulation follows a separate requirement covering residential water heaters. Under the revised timeline, smaller natural gas water heaters will face zero-NOx requirements from January 1, 2028, potentially requiring another round of equipment replacements for affected households.Reducing pollution from residential and commercial buildings is the main goal, but the most recent cost assessment emphasizes the potential infrastructure and financial difficulties.
Article Summary: The Bay Area Air Quality Management District estimates that switching from a conventional gas furnace to an electric heat-pump system could add approximately $12,526 to installation costs for a typical single-family home. The requirement is part of Regulation 9, Rule 4, which aims to eliminate nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions from newly installed natural gas-fired furnaces.

Article Title: Indian-origin man killed in multi-car crash in Arkansas; daughter in ICU as community raises funds for family
Article Text:
Indian-origin man killed in road crash in Arkansas.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A 39-year-old Indian-origin man, Ashok Somasundaram, was killed in a road accident in Bentonville, Arkansas. His two young children were traveling with him. Both of them were injured. According to the Arkansas State Police, the crash occurred on November 21 afternoon at the intersection of SW 14th Street and Tunbridge Drive. A driver allegedly ran a red light and struck another vehicle, which was then pushed into Somasundaram.Arkansas State Police identified the other driver as 22-year-old Javier Edgardo Reyes Orellana. According to witnesses cited by police, he was travelling at a high speed on SW 14th Street when he allegedly ran a red light and struck Ashok's vehicle. The impact sent Ashok's vehicle into an e-bike ridden by 39-year-old Jacob Staly, who died at the scene. Ashok was taken to Mercy Hospital in Rogers, where he later died from his injuries. The other driver remained hospitalized, police said.Somasundaram's nine-year-old daughter is in the ICU and his 4-year-old son suffered minor injuries.The Northwest Arkansas Indian community set up a fundraiser for the family.Calling Ashok a devoted father of two young children and a loving husband of Sathya Gopal, it said that his sudden death has left his family facing an enormous emotional and financial burden, with his wife now having to cope with the loss while caring for their injured children. The fundraiser has been seeking to raise $400,000 to help the family meet the expenses arising from the tragedy. The money will go towards the daughter's ongoing hospital treatment and recovery, Ashok's funeral and memorial expenses, and the family's everyday living costs. The fundraiser also described Ashok as someone who was always willing to help and support people around him, and appealed to the community to stand by his wife and children during this difficult period. As of November 24, the campaign had collected over $295,000 through around 4,000 donations, according to its GoFundMe page.The community has also announced a visitation for Ashok on Tuesday, November 24, from 4 pm to 6 pm CST at Nelson-Berna Funeral Home, 4520 N Crossover Road, Fayetteville, Arkansas.
Article Summary: Ashok Somasundaram, 39, was killed in a road accident in Bentonville, Arkansas. His two young children were traveling with him and were injured. A driver allegedly ran a red light and struck another vehicle, which was then pushed into Ashok.

Article Title: An Ohio woman spent years paying to maintain a Colorado property held for her daughters while her former husband stayed unreachable in Mexico; an appeals court says he must reimburse $101,723.27 after
Article Text:
(AI Image)

Divorce agreement placed property costs on Willard

Former wife struggled to contact him

Willard disputed the repair costs

Lower court initially reduced the payment

Appeals court restores reimbursement

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Attorney fees sent back for reconsideration

An Ohio man must pay his ex-wife $101,723.27 after she spent years covering taxes, insurance, utility bills, and repairs for a Colorado house he was supposed to maintain under their divorce deal. The Ohio Sixth District Court of Appeals overturned a lower court decision that had dropped a contempt ruling against Willard H. Sturt and lowered what he owed. In its 20 November 2026 ruling, the appeals court decided his ex-wife, Diane F. Sturt, had the right to get back the money she spent keeping the Minturn, Colorado, home in good shape.The fight was over a house held for the former couple and their two daughters. Diane told the court that Willard quit paying the home's bills in 2020 and became hard to reach while spending part of the year in Mexico. In its ruling in Sturt v. Sturt, the appeals court found that the original divorce deal put Willard in charge of all costs tied to the house. It also ruled that Diane did not need his okay before setting up needed repairs and paying overdue bills. The court figured that Willard owed her $101,723.27 for insurance, property taxes, utilities, and upkeep, and sent the issue of lawyer fees back to the lower court for another look.Diane and Willard Sturt got married on 12 June 1993 and divorced on 6 January 2015. They have two daughters, born in 1993 and 1996. As part of the divorce deal, the pair agreed to put the Colorado house into a permanent trust for their benefit, with their daughters set to inherit it, and both parents named as co-trustees. The divorce ruling also spelled out how the home's day-to-day costs would be split. According to the court's decision, Willard had to pay all costs tied to the house, including mortgage payments, property taxes, utilities, and upkeep. Diane had to pay him back each year for either half of the real costs or $5,000, whichever was less, once he showed her the bills, invoices, and canceled checks. The deal separately required the pair to split property insurance costs down the middle, with Diane setting up the insurance payments and Willard paying her back for half of the premiums. This setup became the heart of the fight after Diane said Willard quit meeting his money duties.Diane filed a request asking the court to find Willard in contempt on 19 September 2023. She claimed he failed to pay property taxes, insurance bills, utilities, and repair costs, forcing her to cover them. At a hearing on 1 October 2024, Diane told a magistrate that Willard stopped paying the home's bills in late 2020. She said she wrote to him at his Ohio house and tried to reach him through his job, but never got a reply. She testified that some utilities were close to being shut off and that repairs were needed to keep the house from falling apart. According to the judgment, Diane said she paid the past-due bills and set up the needed work because she felt the house had to be protected, turning in invoices and other records proving what she spent. Diane told the court she visited the Colorado home about twice a year, where her daughter and son-in-law had lived for the past two to three years. Willard, on the other hand, had not visited the house since their daughter moved in, according to Diane's testimony.Willard admitted during the hearing that he quit paying the home's bills, including property taxes since 2020 and his share of the insurance. He claimed Diane let their daughter move into the house without asking him, arguing that having someone live full-time in what had been a vacation home drove up running costs and wear and tear. He also questioned how much Diane spent on repairs and criticized the workers she hired. According to the court judgment, Willard said he wanted to do some of the work himself or hire people who helped build the house, though he admitted those original builders were no longer around in the area. He agreed that several parts of the house needed work, including the outside, deck, roof, and heating system, and admitted the deck railings had fallen off and the original fridge was over 20 years old. Willard insisted Diane should have talked to him before setting up the work, claiming he could have gotten some repairs done for less money. The court also heard that Willard had no phone and spent much of his time in Mexico. He admitted getting some letters from Diane, but said she could have reached him on his current wife's phone, even though he acknowledged his wife would not take calls from Diane because the two women did not get along.After the October 2024 hearing, a magistrate found that Willard failed to live up to his duties under the divorce deal. The magistrate figured he owed Diane $40,171.50 for insurance, taxes, utilities, and upkeep, found him in contempt of court, and handed him a 30-day jail term, which he could skip by paying what he owed and the 2024 property taxes by 10 March 2025. The magistrate also granted Diane $5,000 for lawyer fees and $150 for court costs. Both sides fought the ruling. Willard claimed Diane had no right to set up repairs and ask for money back without getting his okay first, while Diane argued the magistrate lowballed her costs and should have counted extra repair, insurance, water, and internet bills. On 23 September 2025, the Lucas County Court of Common Pleas sided partly with Willard by taking the repair costs out of the contempt ruling, saying the divorce deal did not clearly allow Diane to set up repairs on her own and then ask to be paid back. The lower court also wiped out the lawyer fee award and cut the amount of money Willard had to pay, prompting Diane to take her appeal to Ohio's Sixth District Court of Appeals.In its 20 November 2026 decision, the appeals court tossed out the lower court's logic. The judges said the divorce deal clearly put Willard in charge of all costs tied to the Colorado house, and nothing in it required Diane to get his okay before setting up needed upkeep. The court also noted that Willard admitted walking away from his money duties even though he knew repairs and other bills were due, deciding he had purposefully ignored the divorce ruling and that the facts backed up the original contempt finding.The appeals court also rejected the claim that Diane could not get paid back for repair work she set up herself, saying the deal did not let Willard shirk his duties while leaving the house open to unpaid bills and decay. The judges ultimately figured that Willard owed Diane $101,723.27, instead of the $40,171.50 granted by the magistrate. The updated total covered insurance, property taxes, water, internet, and upkeep, adjusted for Diane's own share of the bills, and put the repair costs back into the money terms Willard must pay to clear his contempt charge.The appeals court also took another look at the decision to wipe out Diane's lawyer fee award. It pointed out that the lower court denied the fees partly because it had removed the repair costs from the contempt ruling, so overturning that choice meant the lawyer fee question had to be looked at again. The case was sent back to the trial court to weigh whether granting Diane lawyer fees and legal costs would be fair and decide if another hearing on the matter is needed. The Sixth District Court of Appeals agreed with all five of Diane's points of error and overturned the lower court's September 2025 ruling in its decision, listed as Sturt v. Sturt, 2026-Ohio-4621, which came out on 20 November 2026.
Article Summary: Ohio man must pay his ex-wife $101,723.27 after she spent years covering taxes, insurance, utility bills, and repairs for a Colorado house he was supposed to maintain under their divorce deal. The Ohio Sixth District Court of Appeals overturned a lower court decision that had dropped a contempt ruling against Willard H. Sturt. Diane told the court that Willard quit paying the home's bills in 2020 and became hard to reach while spending part of the year in Mexico.

Article Title: Intruders break into Prince William's country home in major security breach
Article Text:
William, Prince of Wales, and his wife Catherine, Princess of Wales (File photo/PTI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Intruders broke into the country home of Britain's Prince William and his wife, Catherine, according to a report by The Sun newspaper on Tuesday.Police are investigating the break-in at Anmer Hall, located on the royal family's Sandringham estate in Norfolk, eastern England.Neither William, who is first in line to the British throne after his father, King Charles, nor Catherine and their three children were present at the 10-bedroom property at the time of the break-in.Queen Elizabeth II gifted the house to the couple as a wedding present in 2011. She died in 2022, after which her son Charles ascended to the throne.The family's primary residence is on the Windsor Castle estate, west of London. However, they use Anmer Hall as a country retreat for holidays and short breaks.The report came as William visited Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the British leader's office, 10 Downing Street, in London.The latest break-in follows a similar incident in 2024, when two masked burglars broke into Shaw Farm on the Windsor Castle estate. At the time, William, Catherine and their children were sleeping nearby at Adelaide Cottage in Home Park.In May, a man was arrested following an incident at Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's residence on the Sandringham estate. Andrew, William's uncle, was stripped of his royal titles by his elder brother, King Charles, over his links to convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.William and his family receive round-the-clock armed security protection as working members of the British royal family.
Article Summary: Police are investigating the break-in at Anmer Hall, located on the royal family's Sandringham estate in Norfolk. Queen Elizabeth II gifted the house to the couple as a wedding present in 2011. William and his family receive round- the-clock armed security protection as working members of the British royal family.

Article Title: Russia claims strikes on Starlink terminals, drone sites in Ukraine's Sumy
Article Text:
Aftermath of a Russian drone strike in Zaporizhzhia (Photo: Reuters).

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Russia's military struck drone control sites, Starlink satellite terminals and other military assets in Ukraine's Sumy region, while a separate overnight attack on Zaporizhzhia injured 11 people, according to Ukrainian and Russian officials.The Russian defence ministry said its forces had hit the military targets in Sumy, Interfax news agency reported on Tuesday.In Zaporizhzhia, regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said 11 people were injured in the Russian attack, with a woman in serious condition. He warned that people could be trapped under the rubble after strikes damaged apartment buildings, private homes, transport infrastructure and cars.Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia was preparing further attacks and urged people to pay attention to air raid alerts.In a post on X, Zelenskyy said Ukraine's intelligence had indicated that Russia was preparing new strikes. He also called on the United States and other countries supplying anti-ballistic missile interceptors to Ukraine to take the warnings seriously."Every Patriot missile we have is a blow to Russia – a blow to its contempt for diplomacy and for life,"Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine needed more missiles for its Patriot air defence systems.He said the war continued because Russia believed it could "kill and destroy", and urged Washington to take the necessary decisions to provide Ukraine with additional interceptors to protect its cities and infrastructure.
Article Summary: Russia's military struck drone control sites, Starlink satellite terminals and other military assets in Ukraine's Sumy region. A separate overnight attack on Zaporizhzhia injured 11 people, according to Ukrainian and Russian officials. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia was preparing further attacks.

Article Title: Russia planning to launch N-arms into space?
Article Text:
(This is an AFP story)

Nato chief Mark Rutte said Monday the alliance would defend against threats in space when asked about German media reports that Russia may be preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite. Public broadcasters WDR and NDR, along with the Sueddeutsche Zeitung daily, reported that Russia planned to launch a satellite dubbed "Sputnik-S" equipped with a nuclear warhead sometime in the coming weeks.The outlets, citing unnamed sources, said that the intelligence reports about the plans had recently been shared among several Nato countries and that the German govt had been briefed on the matter. The satellite had been stored in the Moscow region, according to the news outlets, and could be used to disrupt or destroy important communications and observation satellites orbiting Earth. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the latest news stories on the topic but that frequent reports citing "unknown sources" are "hardly worth taking seriously".
Article Summary: Nato chief Mark Rutte says alliance will defend against threats in space. German media reports that Russia may be preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov says frequent reports citing "unknown sources" are "hardly worth taking seriously"

Article Title: ‘Justice is not for sale’: California governor Newsom demands federal reforms to limit presidential pardon powers
Article Text:
Newsom targets Trump over pardons, alleges clemency has become a business under his watch

Trump hits back at Newsom

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

California governor Gavin Newsom has called for sweeping federal reforms to the US president's power to grant pardons, accusing President Donald Trump of using the Justice Department to protect wealthy allies and politically connected individuals.He alleged that clemency had become a business under the Trump administration.In a post on X, Newsom said, "No president should be able to sell a pardon. Today, I’m calling for sweeping federal reform of the presidential pardon power. The Justice Department is not Donald Trump’s personal law firm. Justice is NOT for sale."In a video message accompanying the post, Newsom criticised MAGA supremo for delivering remarks at the department of justice (DOJ) alongside Attorney General Pam Bondi, who previously served as his personal defence lawyer."Today, Donald Trump is once again standing inside the Department of Justice next to his former personal defence lawyer, who is now the Attorney General, giving a speech about protecting American families," Newsom said.Questioning Trump's record on criminal justice, Newsom referred to the 1989 case involving five Black and Latino teenagers who were wrongfully accused of raping and assaulting a woman in New York's Central Park.The teenagers, later known as the Central Park Five, were exonerated after DNA evidence and a confession by another individual established their innocence."In 1989, you took out full-page ads screaming for the death penalty for five Black and Latino teenagers before a trial, before a shred of evidence. They were innocent. DNA proved it. You never apologised," Newsom said.The California governor also defended his own clemency decisions, insisting that individuals on the state's former death row would remain behind bars for life."To the families standing with him today, your grief is real. That's why every person, every person on California's former death row will die in prison. No one walks out," he said, contrasting his approach with Trump's use of presidential pardons.Newsom alleged that several individuals convicted of serious offences had received presidential pardons after making financial contributions or benefiting from personal connections involving Trump's political circle.Citing specific cases, he alleged that a billionaire facing bribery charges had secured a pardon after his family arranged a $50 million deal involving Trump's lawyer. He also claimed that an individual convicted of stealing $10 million from nursing home workers received clemency after his mother attended a million-dollar dinner at Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.Newsom also criticised Trump's decision to pardon former Blackwater security contractors convicted in connection with the 2007 killing of 14 Iraqi civilians, including two children, in Baghdad.He further referred to the pardon of a participant in the January 6 Capitol riot who subsequently pleaded guilty to soliciting what he believed was a 15-year-old girl for sex. Newsom also criticised Trump's pardon of a foreign leader accused of facilitating large-scale cocaine trafficking into the United States."Nearly two billion, nearly $2 billion owed to victims and their families, gone. His own pardon attorney said it out loud: 'No MAGA left behind'," Newsom alleged.Accusing Trump of applying different standards of justice based on an individual's wealth and political connections, Newsom said, "Donald Trump doesn't oppose mercy. He sells it. If you're poor, Black, or Brown, you get the needle. If you're rich and know Donald Trump, you get a pardon and a personal phone call."He also raised concerns over Trump's remarks suggesting that more pardons could be forthcoming, including his statement that the possibility of pardoning himself was not unreasonable."A Justice Department that prosecutes his enemies and pardons himself and his friends? That's not law enforcement. That's a protection racket," Newsom said.Calling for structural changes to presidential clemency powers, Newsom said reforms were needed to prevent future presidents from using their constitutional authority to grant pardons for personal or financial benefit."We need foundational federal reform, starting with this: no president can ever again turn the power of mercy into a business. No president and no one should be able to sell a pardon," he said.Concluding his video message, the California governor reiterated that the Justice Department must function independently and serve the American people."A Justice Department is not Donald Trump's law firm. Justice is not for sale--not in California, and not in America," Newsom added.Newsom's remarks came after Trump sharply criticised the California Governor over his decision to grant clemency to 548 death row inmates, including individuals convicted of murdering children.Speaking at the Department of Justice on Monday (local time), Trump described Newsom's decision as one of the most shocking acts of injustice in the country. He accused the Governor and what he termed the Radical Left of prioritising convicted criminals over victims and their families."We're here today to talk about one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country has ever seen... Just days ago, the Governor of California, Gavin Newsom, granted clemency and mercy to 548 of the most EVIL monsters on the face of the Earth," Trump said.The US President also announced a Presidential Directive ordering the DOJ to seek the death penalty for individuals convicted of murdering children, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims."I will sign a Presidential Directive ordering the DOJ to seek the death penalty for child murderers, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims. My order also directs the Attorney General to expedite the execution of federal death sentences. Once juries have spoken, capital punishment will be swift and certain," Trump said.He also referred to an executive order signed on the first day of his administration, directing the DOJ to pursue capital punishment for individuals convicted of murdering law enforcement officers.Trump further announced nearly $150 million in public safety grants to support the recruitment of more than 1,000 additional sworn law enforcement officers and improve responses to domestic violence and sexual assault cases.Additionally, he backed a legislative proposal introduced by Representative Brandon Gill, titled the 'Just Punishment for Murder Act'.The proposal seeks to strengthen capital punishment provisions and expand their application to individuals convicted of murdering law enforcement officers and illegal immigrants accused of murder.
Article Summary: California governor Gavin Newsom has called for sweeping federal reforms to the US president's power to grant pardons. He accused President Donald Trump of using the Justice Department to protect wealthy allies and politically connected individuals. Newsom's remarks came after Trump sharply criticised the California Governor over his decision to grant clemency to 548 death row inmates.

Article Title: Sheikh Hasina requests December 16 return, picks Bangladesh Victory Day for comeback
Article Text:
File photo: Former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina

Hasina seeks return as Dhaka presses India for extradition

Also read:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Ousted Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina has set December 16 as the date for her return from India. Specifically choosing the anniversary of her country's victory in the 1971 liberation war to make her way back to Dhaka, where the Tarique Rahman-led government has warned she will be arrested and jailed.Hasina, who has been living in exile in India since fleeing Bangladesh in August 2024, announced her plan through a spokesperson on Tuesday. It is the first time she has named a specific date for her return, potentially escalating an already tense standoff between her banned Awami League party and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party-led government.In a statement, Hasina called on Dhaka to arrange her return on the national flag carrier, Biman Bangladesh Airlines, saying she had left the country aboard a Bangladeshi aircraft on August 5, 2024.“Having exiled her contrary to the Constitution under such circumstances, it is now the responsibility of the government to make possible her return to Bangladesh on Victory Day on December 16th,” spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali said to Reuters.The Bangladeshi government has, however, made clear that Hasina, who faces a death sentence in her home country, would be arrested upon arrival. State minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed told Reuters previously that she would be taken to jail and the law would take its course.“We would like India to honour the extradition treaty and return her as a convict,” Obaed said, adding that Hasina would have to face the consequences of her conviction.Hasina fled to New Delhi after a student-led uprising toppled her government, bringing an end to her 15-year rule. The United Nations has estimated that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.Bangladesh’s war crimes tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in absentia in November 2025 for crimes against humanity linked to the crackdown on the uprising. She has rejected the verdict as politically motivated.Earlier this month, Hasina sought a new passport and other identity documents, which had been cancelled after she left the country. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party-led government rejected her applications.Hasina had previously said in August that she intended to return by December, but Tuesday’s statement marks the first time she has identified a precise date.Bangladesh has also been hit by a fresh wave of violence and political unrest in Bangladesh. The Awami League, which was banned by the interim administration led by Muhammad Yunus, has called for nationwide protests in support of Hasina.Obaed described the attacks as an attempt by a “politically bankrupt” Awami League to survive, while also rejecting reports that India had set conditions for Hasina’s extradition.She said there had been no official discussions with New Delhi about arranging an aircraft to bring Hasina back, and stressed that Bangladesh wanted relations with India that respected its “dignity, self-respect and interests”.India has repeatedly said that Dhaka’s extradition request for Hasina remains under consideration.
Article Summary: Sheikh Hasina has been living in exile in India since fleeing Bangladesh in August 2024. She has chosen the anniversary of her country's victory in the 1971 liberation war to make her way back to Dhaka. The Bangladeshi government has, however, made clear that Hasina, who faces a death sentence in her home country, would be arrested upon arrival.

Article Title: New Haven agrees to pay $30 million to George Gould, who spent nearly 27 years in prison, and the estate of Ronald Taylor, who died in 2011, after their convictions in a 1993 murder were thrown out
Article Text:
New Haven's $30 million settlement awaits committee review and Board of Alders approval for borrowing.

Two men convicted in a 1993 murder

A lengthy legal battle before exoneration

$30 million settlement and approval process

Wrongful-conviction settlements reach $77 million

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

More lawsuits remain unresolved

Nearly three decades behind bars, a conviction that unravelled years later and a settlement worth millions of dollars have brought two wrongful-conviction cases in Connecticut closer to a conclusion. The city of New Haven has agreed to pay $30 million to George Gould and the estate of Ronald Taylor, who were imprisoned for a 1993 murder they did not commit. While Gould will receive $18 million after spending almost 27 years incarcerated, Taylor's estate is set to receive $12 million following his death in 2011. The settlement, reported by the New Haven Independent and Hartford Courant, marks another major financial resolution for the city as it faces mounting lawsuits linked to wrongful convictions dating back several decades.Gould and Taylor were convicted of felony murder and other charges in connection with the July 4, 1993, killing of Eugenia Vega inside her Grand Avenue bodega in New Haven.According to the New Haven Independent, the prosecution's case relied heavily on testimony from a woman who claimed to have witnessed the crime. She later revealed that she had been arrested for prostitution and interrogated while experiencing severe heroin withdrawal.She alleged that police offered to help her obtain heroin in exchange for providing the statement they wanted. Investigators reportedly found no physical evidence linking either Gould or Taylor to the killing.Years later, two relatives reportedly approached the FBI and said Vega's son had confessed to them that he had killed his father, bringing fresh scrutiny to the convictions.The men's legal struggle involved multiple court proceedings. In 2010, a Connecticut Superior Court judge granted their habeas corpus petitions on grounds of actual innocence and ordered their release.However, the state appealed, and the Connecticut Supreme Court subsequently overturned that decision. During a second habeas proceeding, their petitions were denied, the online report adds.Gould returned to prison in 2011, while Taylor was allowed to remain at home because of his terminal cancer diagnosis. He died in October 2011, after spending more than 16 years incarcerated, New Haven Independent reported.Gould continued challenging his conviction and was released in 2021 after a judge modified his sentence. The state's Conviction Integrity Unit later reviewed the case, and prosecutors moved to vacate both convictions in 2024.The agreement was reached on November 13 in two consolidated federal civil rights cases against the city, the report added.Under the settlement, Gould will receive $18 million, while Taylor's estate, administered by Mary Murphy-Taylor, will receive $12 million. The latter payment remains subject to approval by the New Haven Probate Court.According to the Hartford Courant, the agreement also requires approval from the city's Litigation Settlement Committee. The New Haven Board of Alders must subsequently approve borrowing for the settlement.The New Haven Independent reported that Gould's legal representatives include Neufeld Scheck Brustin Hoffmann & Freudenberger, the Law Offices of Richard Emanuel and the Law Office of Attorney Michael A. Jefferson.The latest agreement represents the fourth and fifth federal civil rights lawsuits New Haven has settled within three months. Earlier settlements involved Adam Carmon for $16.5 million, Vernon Horn for $15.25 million and Marquis Jackson for $15.25 million.Together, the five settlements total $77 million. According to city officials cited by the New Haven Independent and Hartford Courant, borrowing to finance the payments could result in at least $116 million in repayments over 20 years when interest is included.Mayor Justin Elicker has acknowledged the city's responsibility to address past injustices while raising concerns about the financial burden on taxpayers. He has also called for the state to share more of the costs, noting that state authorities appealed the original decision granting Gould and Taylor relief.The mayor's office has pointed to the city's lack of insurance coverage for this type of incident in 1993 and the financial implications of settling claims decades later.The financial consequences may not end with the latest agreement. According to the New Haven Independent, lawsuits involving former Alder Troy Streater and Charles Coleman Jr. remain outstanding, alongside the separate case involving Stefon Morant, in which a jury previously awarded $38 million against the city. New Haven is appealing that verdict.For Gould, the settlement brings an end to a legal struggle that continued long after his release. For Taylor's family, the compensation comes years after his death and the eventual overturning of his conviction.The agreement represents another step in addressing wrongful convictions from New Haven's past, while leaving the city to confront the continuing legal and financial consequences.Image Courtesy: George Gould (right), with the late Ronald Taylor (center). Credit: Thomas MacMillan photo
Article Summary: The city of New Haven has agreed to pay $30 million to George Gould and the estate of Ronald Taylor, who were imprisoned for a 1993 murder they did not commit. Gould will receive $18 million after spending almost 27 years incarcerated, while Taylor's estate is set to receive $12 million following his death in 2011. The settlement marks another major financial resolution for the city as it faces mounting lawsuits linked to wrongful convictions dating back several decades.

Article Title: A Las Vegas Strip parking-lot owner installed a chain-link fence and QR-code gates, restricting access for a neighbouring shopping centre's customers; Nevada's top court upheld an order to remove the
Article Text:
Chain-link fence and QR-code gates restricting access to a Las Vegas Strip parking lot. (AI image)

New gates disrupt access to shopping centre

Lower court backs shopping centre

Owner argues some access was still available

Shopping centre warns of impact on tenants

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Court rejects owner's safety concerns

A dispute over customer parking on the Las Vegas Strip has ended with the state's Supreme Court backing an order on Friday to remove a fence and electronic gates installed around a vacant parking lot. The property owner had enclosed the land with a chain-link fence and introduced a QR-code system for motorists who wanted to park there. However, a neighbouring shopping centre said the changes interfered with access its customers were entitled to under an existing agreement. The Nevada Supreme Court upheld a lower court's order directing the owner to take down the barriers from the portion of the property covered by the agreement.According to CREdocket, a legal news website, the disagreement involves two companies that own neighbouring properties on the Las Vegas Strip. One operates a vacant parking lot, while the other owns a shopping centre housing retail outlets and restaurants. The shopping centre's owner, EC 215 Las Vegas LLC, is referred to as Silver City in the court documents. It argued that the new entry arrangements made it difficult for its customers to reach the shopping centre.The issue arose after Siegel LV North Strip Tolleson LLC bought the parking lot. The purchase came with an existing agreement that allowed Silver City and its customers to use certain parts of the land. Siegel later introduced the fence and gates, prompting the shopping centre to challenge the changes in court.The parking lot was not entirely free of obligations when Siegel acquired it. An agreement known as the Parking Easement Agreement gave Silver City and its customers access to specified sections of the property.Siegel subsequently enclosed the lot with a chain-link fence. It also installed gates that required customers arriving by car to enter a QR code to park without paying.The new arrangement changed how people could move between the parking lot and the neighbouring shopping centre. Customers could no longer freely use the lot as a route to reach Silver City's property. The court order noted that the barriers affected both pedestrians and motorists.Silver City objected, saying the changes went against the access arrangement already in place. It approached the district court and asked for an order requiring Siegel to remove the fencing and gates.The company argued that the restrictions could also affect its shopping centre tenants, whose customers needed access to parking facilities.The dispute first reached the Eighth Judicial District Court in Clark County. After hearing evidence from both sides, the court sided with Silver City at the preliminary stage of the case.On July 10, 2024, it ordered Siegel to remove the barriers while the legal proceedings continued. This was a temporary measure intended to protect the shopping centre's access rights until the wider dispute could be resolved.Siegel asked the district court to reconsider its decision. The request was rejected on April 28, 2025. However, the court clarified that the company did not have to remove the entire fencing arrangement. The direction applied only to the sections covered by the parking agreement. Siegel then challenged the order before Nevada's Supreme Court.Siegel's main argument was that the agreement did not prevent it from putting up barriers around its property. The company maintained that Silver City had been given access to the parking lot, but that this did not mean customers had to be allowed to enter and move through it without restrictions.In other words, Siegel argued that the QR-code gates did not necessarily violate the agreement because customers could still gain access through the system. The Supreme Court did not accept this as sufficient reason to overturn the lower court's order.The judges considered the agreement and the district court's assessment of the dispute. They found that allowing some access was not the same as complying with all the access rights available to Silver City under the agreement.The court also considered Siegel's argument that certain restrictions in the agreement applied only when construction of a parking garage began. It found that this did not establish that the company was free to block or restrict access before construction started.The Supreme Court did not make a final ruling on every disagreement over the meaning of the agreement. It examined whether the lower court had reasonable grounds to believe Silver City could succeed in its case and needed protection while the proceedings continued. It found no sufficient reason to interfere with that decision.Siegel also questioned why the shopping centre needed a court order when any financial losses could potentially be recovered through compensation.Silver City argued that the consequences of restricted parking could go beyond lost business or reduced revenue. Its agreements with shopping centre tenants included responsibilities relating to parking access for their customers.If the barriers remained, the shopping centre could face difficulties meeting those commitments. This could affect its business relationships with the retailers and restaurants operating on the property.The Supreme Court considered this a significant concern. It agreed that the potential damage was not limited to losses that could easily be calculated and repaid later.The judges therefore found that the district court had sufficient evidence to conclude that financial compensation alone might not address the problem.Siegel also suggested that the gates could have been modified instead of being removed. The company argued that changes to the system might have allowed customers to reach the shopping centre while keeping some restrictions around the parking lot.However, it did not point to any particular alternative that the lower court had failed to consider. Silver City had sought the removal of the barriers, and the district court had granted that request for the areas covered by the agreement.The Supreme Court said its decision did not prevent the parties from discussing a modified arrangement during the continuing legal proceedings.Siegel further argued that removing the fence and gates could create problems for the parking lot, including concerns involving crime and homelessness.The company wanted these risks to be considered while deciding whether the barriers should remain in place.However, the Supreme Court pointed out that Siegel had known about these concerns when it purchased the property. It said the company could not use problems that already existed at the time of purchase as a reason to justify installing the barriers later. After examining the arguments, the court found no grounds to overturn the district court's order.
Article Summary: Nevada Supreme Court upholds lower court's order to remove barriers. Dispute involves two companies that own neighbouring properties on the Las Vegas Strip. One operates a vacant parking lot, while the other owns a shopping centre. Property owner enclosed the land with a chain-link fence and introduced a QR- code system for motorists who wanted to park there.

Article Title: A Florida lawyer vanished from his office in 2023, leaving his keys and phone behind; three years later, the plastic surgeon convicted of killing him was sentenced to death, but his body remains missi
Article Text:

Sudden disappearance raised suspicion

A calculated killing and a missing body

Evidence that sealed the prosecution's case

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Death sentence despite mitigating circumstances

A lawyer walked into his office one morning and seemingly vanished without a trace. His phone, wallet and keys were left behind, his computer remained open, and there was no indication that he had planned to leave. Nearly three years later, the mystery surrounding his disappearance reached a grim legal conclusion, with a Florida judge sentencing the man convicted of killing him to death. Yet, despite the conviction, the lawyer’s body has never been recovered. The case of attorney Steven Cozzi and plastic surgeon Dr Tomasz Kosowski exposed a disturbing chain of events involving a bitter professional dispute, a meticulously planned killing and an unsuccessful search for human remains.Cozzi left personal items behind when he left his Florida law office in March 2023.Her husband hadn’t heard from him and this sudden disappearance was making him worried.According to AP News, investigators later established that Cozzi had been killed inside the bathroom of his workplace, shortly after participating in a conference call connected to a prolonged legal dispute. Cozzi represented a medical practice based in Dunedin, Florida, which had been involved in an acrimonious disagreement with Kosowski.The plastic surgeon alleged that the practice had withheld thousands of dollars in billing payments and damaged his professional reputation.Prosecutors argued that Kosowski had prepared extensively before carrying out the murder. He reportedly participated in the conference call from a Toyota pickup truck parked outside the office before entering the building.Investigators said he had brought supplies including trash bags, a syringe containing a paralysing drug and a wagon to transport the body.US News reported that authorities used cellphone records and surveillance footage to trace Kosowski's movements towards a remote stretch of the Tamiami Trail, west of Miami. Investigators believe he disposed of Cozzi's body in a rubbish container that was subsequently emptied by a garbage truck. The truck driver reportedly noticed an unusually foul smell during the collection.Authorities later searched a Collier County landfill where rubbish from the route was believed to have been transported. However, the facility's routine waste-compaction process made recovering the remains virtually impossible.Although Cozzi's body remains missing, investigators uncovered substantial forensic evidence. His blood and DNA were discovered in the bathroom of the law office and inside the garage at Kosowski's residence.The Independent reported that investigators also found a significant collection of weapons and suspicious equipment when Kosowski was arrested. These included approximately $280,000 in cash, firearms, masks, duct tape, a ballistic vest marked EMS, law enforcement patches and a vial of succinylcholine, a paralysing drug. Court documents also indicated that around 200 guns were recovered from his home.Kosowski was convicted in September after representing himself during the trial. He presented no substantive defence, maintaining during his closing argument that prosecutors had failed to establish his guilt.On Thursday, Pinellas Circuit Judge Joseph Bulone sentenced Kosowski to death, choosing capital punishment over life imprisonment without the possibility of release.A court-appointed special counsel said Kosowski graduated from Dartmouth College medical school and specialized in reconstructive breast surgery. The judge deemed the murder's premeditation more significant than these mitigating factors. The public defender's office has been appointed to represent Kosowski in his appeals.For Cozzi's family, the sentence marks a significant development, but not complete closure. Nearly three years after his disappearance, the question of where his body lies remains unanswered.Image Courtesy: Google Gemini
Article Summary: Steven Cozzi disappeared from his Florida law office in March 2023. Dr Tomasz Kosowski was convicted in September after representing himself and arguing that prosecutors had failed to prove his guilt. Despite the conviction, the lawyer’s body has never been recovered.

The Cultural Impact of GTA VI

Thirteen years separated GTA V and GTA VI. The world witnessed a pandemic, Messi winning the World Cup, Donald Trump winning two presidential elections and the rise of generative AI. Yet GTA V remained among YouTube’s ten most-viewed games every year from 2013 to 2025.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Times They Are A-Changin’

In British politics in the early noughties, it was said that the most terrifying words in the political lexicon were: “Michael Crick is in reception.” The words reflected the sheer terror generated in British political circles by the “terrier-like reputation” of Crick, whose journalism, combining unstinting principles with inexhaustible research, made even the most seasoned politicians, used to the most putrid tabloids, quake in their boots.But the times change, and those who don’t change with the times are often the subject of some ridicule, as Crick learned when he tweeted his outrage about GTA VI on the BBC, calling it a “ridiculous puff (piece)” and “appalling free advertising”.Crick’s diatribe led Piers Morgan, a man who moves with the alacrity of a bloodhound pouncing upon any outrage, to rebut him with “Calm down, Grandpa”.Now we live in a hyperconnected world, where we face being labelled outcasts, where one can be mocked for not weighing in on the ending of, being excited about, or explaining why the first few soporific episodes ofare worth the wait.But even by those exalted standards, GTA VI seems to have become a hitherto unseen cultural phenomenon that has consumed everything in its wake.The blurb of JRR Tolkien’sused to read: “The English-speaking world is divided into those who have read Lord of the Rings, and those who are going to read Lord of the Rings.” The same applies to GTA VI: even if not everyone plays the game, everyone will be part of the conversation.Now, if, like Crick, you are scratching your head about how a video game with a grammatically wonky (but legally sound) title became a global phenomenon, here’s a primer.There was a time when gamers were often chided by their mothers for wasting time on video games. Today, it’s usually their wives doing the chiding, but it’s kind of ironic given that Nvidia’s chips, from a company that cut its teeth by making GPUs for gaming nerds, are the foundation upon which the modern AI frontier model race is built.To understand the GTA phenomenon, we have to take a small walk through the history of video games, which, in popular imagination, started with two white rectangles hitting a white dot across a black screen. That might sound like an exaggeration, but that’s one of the earliest commercially successful video games, called, released by Atari in 1972. The graphics became better with time, with a dot becoming a spaceship in(1978) and a yellow circle in(1980). Then came the gaming console era, where aeons were wasted getting an Italian plumber or a parkour-loving prince to rescue a pixelated princess.Soon, gaming moved from addictive pixels in a 2D world to a more open space.At this time, a company in Scotland named DMA Design, founded by David Jones, developed a game called Race ‘n’ Chase that involved police officers pursuing criminals. That turned out to be inordinately, mind-numbingly boring, so the company flipped the script and made the criminal the protagonist, andwas first released in 1997.And thus we got the most famous Scottish export since whisky and Sean Connery, with each open world based on a real city. The game arrived at a time when politicians discovered that, rather than take responsibility, video games, along with rock music, comic books and television, could be blamed for the moral degradation of society. They were certainly helped by notorious British publicist Max Clifford , who understood that the easiest way to sell something was to get elected officials to deride it. GTA was discussed in the House of Lords – which, given its antecedents, would be a perfect location for a GTA spinoff – and got the kind of publicity money cannot buy.Onscreen, the revolution happened when GTA went from a bird’s-eye, two-dimensional Flatland look to a full three-dimensional open world with GTA III, where one could do everything one wants to do in the real world but cannot because one’s constitution is too delicate for jail: run over pedestrians, sell drugs and do other things that are frowned upon in civil society.The latest instalment, GTA VI, takes us back to Vice City, a fictional version of Miami in the state of Leonida, Rockstar’s take on Florida where all the folks are doing things that allows us to create the Florida man headlines.This time the protagonists are couple Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos. Jason is a former soldier and Lucia GTA’s first female protagonist which is enough to heckle incels across the world. And much like its predecessors, the actual storyline is only part of the attraction, since players are free to ignore it and spend their time doing whatever they please, provided the game's creators have programmed it.While explaining the much-debated100 Greatest TV Shows of the 21st Century, the Times’ chief television critic James Poniewozik explained thatdidn’t make the cut because it premiered in 1999, but its legacy was writ large in the antihero dramas that made the cut, including its top three offerings:and. The same goes for the GTA series, where we’ve overwhelmingly batted for the chance to roleplay as deeply problematic protagonists without having to pay for our sins, as Plato explored all those centuries ago inthrough the story of the Ring of Gyges, which would appear to be an inspiration for Gollum and the LOTR ring.One could even go further and say that the current state of the world, where the most powerful nation is led by a self-aggrandising leader who doesn’t even pretend to couch his avarice in terms of politesse, as was the norm in politics before, is beginning to resemble a live-action version of GTA.Now every qualitative assessment can come down to a quantitative measure, particularly when a video game gets the sort of attention normally reserved for a World Cup final, a general election result or the death of a monarch.The numbers make for remarkable reading.When GTA V was released in September 2013 , it earned over $800 million in retail sales within 24 hours and crossed the billion-dollar mark in three days, making it the fastest entertainment product in history to reach that milestone.For context,, which involved the combined efforts of nearly every superhero Marvel had managed to assemble over a decade, took five days to reach $1 billion at the box office.GTA VI, released on November 19, 2026, made those figures look like petty change.According to Rockstar Games , GTA VI generated $3.79 billion in worldwide retail sales on its first day, including pre-orders, with 32.5 million copies sold before release. GTA VI, meanwhile, had already sold a staggering 32.5 million copies before it was even released. GTA V sold 235 million copies since 2013, taking the total number of copies, including GTA VI pre-sales, to approximately 512 million.YouTube states that content related to the GTA franchise has accumulated 900 billion views on the platform, while GTA VI-related videos attracted 40 billion views before the game hit the shelves.The release itself attracted 7.91 million concurrent viewers across livestreaming platforms, with gamers collectively watching more than 125 million hours of GTA VI streams in the first 24 hours.But perhaps the most astonishing number is13 years separated GTA V and GTA VI. When the former was released, Barack Obama was US president, Narendra Modi was the chief minister of Gujarat, Manchester United were serial Premier League winners, and the idea of a former reality star upending the world order was laughable.But perhaps the metric that shows GTA’s stickiness is the fact that between 2013 and 2025, GTA V remained among YouTube’s ten most-viewed games every single year. In a world where it’s almost impossible to remember what happened between two seasons – and can anyone really tell the Targaryen siblings apart in? – GTA maintained its cultural relevance.Even before GTA VI dropped, the cultural impact of the game became evident. The moment the first trailer came out, featuring Tom Petty’s 1989 song Love Is a Long Road , the song saw a 36,979% surge in Spotify streams, eventually crossing 40 million streams. The first trailer on YouTube racked up 93 million views in 24 hours and a total of over 310 million views.In India, which has an estimated 550 million gamers , mostly on mobile games, GTA VI was released on the PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, making it inaccessible to anyone who didn’t own a compatible console or have access to one. Yet, on the day of its release, gaming cafés across the country were jam-packed , with many taking leave from work to play.Like all things on the internet, it also immediately became a cultural flashpoint, with many complaining that GTA VI was too sanitised because it forces the protagonist to fix sinks, go on dates and even work out, things that people log in to their video games to avoid doing in the real world.Influential streamer Asmongold complained about having to repair a sink, rub Lucia's feet and listen to her friends' stories, while others complained that the game had become too 'woke'. A game that was once deemed to be responsible for moral degradation in the real world was now being accused of replicating it too exactly.The game's most enduring contribution to internet culture, however, might be the meme “We got this before GTA VI” , which became a shorthand for events that nobody thought would happen before the game was released.In the thirteen years between GTA V and GTA VI, we witnessed a global pandemic, the death of Queen Elizabeth II, Messi winning the World Cup, Donald Trump winning the White House twice, and the rise of generative AI, which means that humanity managed to create machines capable of writing poetry, generating videos and replacing white-collar workers before Rockstar managed to release another GTA. The meme became so popular that when GTA VI finally arrived, internet users started mourning its demise, while some pointed out that we had even got the end of the “We got this before GTA VI” meme before GTA VI.Brands, governments and even military alliances decided to jump on the bandwagon. Singapore wondered why folks couldn’t remember the MRT map. Miami police reminded gamers that, unlike the game, their city had rules. KFC had a mock funeral for “Ann Alibi”. The White House released a GTA-inspired video while PM Narendra Modi used GTA V vs GTA VI to highlight the Centre’s developmental work.Twenty-nine years after politicians worried about the moral degradation caused by a fictional world, that world’s cultural baggage had become too much for the real world to ignore. One wonders what Max Clifford, who understood the value of manufacturing outrage, would have made of a world where prime ministers, presidents and military alliances were doing Rockstar’s publicity for free.As Bob Dylan warned in: “Your sons and your daughters are beyond your command.” Six decades later, the parents and politicians seem to have finally got the message.Now it’s their turn to sing the children’s tune.
Article Summary: GTA V sold 235 million copies, while GTA VI recorded 32.5 million pre-release sales. GTA-related content has amassed 900 billion YouTube views, including 40 billion for GTA VI before its launch. GTA V remained among YouTube’s ten most- viewed games every year from 2013 to 2025.

Article Title: A Texas mother with Alzheimer's left her home to her daughter in a 2007 will, but her son used a power of attorney to deed himself a share for $10; an appeals court ruled the transfer invalid
Article Text:

A 2007 will left the Arlington home to the daughter

Medical evidence raised questions about the power of attorney

Appeals court upholds the invalidation of the deed

A family dispute over a Texas woman's home has ended with an appeals court upholding a ruling that invalidated a property transfer made by her son using a power of attorney. The mother, Betty Lou Casey, had left her Arlington residence to her daughter in a 2007 will. Years later, her son, Danny Prine, used a power of attorney purportedly granted by his mother to transfer the property to himself and her for a stated consideration of just $10. In an opinion filed on November 19, 2026, available on Justia, the Texas Eleventh Court of Appeals affirmed the probate court's decision, finding that Casey lacked the mental capacity to execute the power of attorney on which the transfer depended.Casey had three children: Sheila Fisher, Danny Prine and Sherry Neustupa. Her will, dated August 7, 2007, named Fisher as the independent executor of her estate and specifically left her Tarrant County residence on Milby Road in Arlington to her. The remainder of her estate was to be divided equally among the three children.Casey had also signed a durable power of attorney in 2007, naming Fisher as her agent. However, on November 21, 2014, she executed another power of attorney that designated Prine as her agent and Sherry as the alternative agent.Casey had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 2014. Her condition gradually deteriorated, and she died on November 13, 2021, aged 92.During the probate process, Fisher discovered that her brother had executed a warranty deed on February 5, 2021, using the 2014 power of attorney. The document purported to convey the Arlington property to Prine and Casey as joint tenants for a stated consideration of $10. The deed did not contain survivorship language. Prine later re-recorded the deed on July 14, 2022, after Fisher had demanded that he leave the property.Fisher challenged the validity of the 2014 power of attorney and the subsequent property deed. She argued that their mother did not have the mental capacity to execute the document that authorised Prine to act on her behalf. During the trial, Casey's treating physician, Dr Joe Perryman III, testified that he had treated her from 2013 to 2020. She had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and dementia in 2014 and was prescribed medications for cognitive decline. Her primary symptom was memory loss, and her condition progressively worsened.Casey's grandson also testified that he had noticed her memory problems as early as 2011. By 2014, she was increasingly confused, sometimes unable to remember what had happened the previous day, and could no longer manage her finances or prepare meals independently. Fisher described similar changes, saying their mother frequently forgot to pay bills, misplaced belongings and sometimes forgot to eat. She had also begun helping Casey with meals, shopping and medical appointments.An important part of the evidence came from Prine himself. On November 21, 2014, the same day Casey signed the power of attorney naming him as her agent, he had submitted a sworn statement in another estate matter describing his mother as incapacitated because of dementia and unable to manage her affairs. Although Prine later testified that Casey appeared lucid when she signed the document, the probate court found that she lacked the necessary mental capacity.The probate court ruled on March 6, 2025, that the 2014 power of attorney was invalid, the February 2021 deed was invalid, and full ownership of the Arlington property vested in Fisher immediately upon Casey's death. Prine challenged the decision, arguing that the evidence did not establish his mother's incapacity and that the court had wrongly invalidated the deed. He also raised complaints about his sister's handling of the estate.The appeals court rejected his arguments. It explained that the evidence was sufficient to support the finding that Casey did not understand the nature and consequences of signing the 2014 power of attorney. It also noted that Prine's own sworn statement about her incapacity, made on the very day she signed the document, supported that conclusion.The court further explained that a transaction in which an agent transfers property to himself is presumed unfair under the applicable fiduciary principles, placing the burden on the agent to demonstrate that it was fair. Because Prine's authority rested on a power of attorney executed when Casey lacked the required mental capacity, the subsequent deed was voidable. The court found that Fisher had filed the action within the applicable four-year limitation period. On November 19, 2026, the Eleventh Court of Appeals affirmed the probate court's judgment, leaving Fisher with full ownership of the Milby Road property under her mother's will.
Article Summary: Betty Lou Casey left her Arlington residence to her daughter in a 2007 will. Her son, Danny Prine, used a power of attorney purportedly granted by his mother to transfer the property to himself and her for a stated consideration of just $10. Prine challenged the decision, arguing that the evidence did not establish his mother's incapacity. The Texas Eleventh Court of Appeals affirmed the probate court's decision, finding that Casey lacked the mental capacity to execute the power ofAttorney.

Article Title: A New York worker fell while cleaning siding from a rental building's roof after leaving his safety harness at home, but judges said the landlord still had to provide protection and upheld a liability

Why the court held the landlord responsible

Landlord's attempt to recover damages from worker rejected
