A New York landlord has been held liable after a worker fell from the roof of a rental property while cleaning its exterior siding, even though he had left his personal safety harness at home. An appeals court ruled that the property owner was responsible for providing proper fall protection and could not avoid liability by blaming the worker's decision to proceed without his own equipment.The ruling was upheld by the Appellate Division of the New York State Supreme Court, which affirmed an earlier decision granting partial summary judgment to the injured worker, Benjamin E. Irwin, under the state's Labor Law Section 240(1).Irwin was cleaning vinyl siding on a rental building owned by the defendant when he fell from its roof. He was not using any safety equipment at the time of the accident.The landlord challenged the liability ruling, arguing that the work amounted to routine maintenance and therefore did not qualify for protection under the state law. He also maintained that Irwin's own actions were responsible for the accident because he had left his personal safety harness at home.The appeals court rejected both arguments, finding that the cleaning work involved risks similar to those encountered at construction sites and fell within the protection offered by Section 240(1).Under New York's Labor Law Section 240(1), property owners and contractors must provide appropriate safety equipment to protect workers undertaking jobs involving elevation-related hazards.The court noted that although ordinary household window cleaning is generally excluded from the law, other cleaning activities can qualify when they involve comparable risks to construction work.Referring to an earlier ruling in Soto v J. Crew Inc., the judges said cleaning projects must be assessed according to their circumstances, rather than automatically being classified as routine maintenance.In Irwin's case, the court found that the landlord had failed to provide any safety devices despite the risk involved in working at height. It also noted that the property contained at least three rental units, making the owner subject to the statutory safety obligations.The judges said the landlord could not transfer that responsibility to the worker simply because he had chosen to use his own equipment.They also rejected the argument that Irwin should have cleaned the difficult-to-reach sections from second-floor windows instead of climbing onto the roof.The court explained that choosing one method of completing a job over another, even when a safer alternative might have been available, amounts to comparative negligence. That alone does not remove an owner's liability under Section 240(1).The judges found that this defence could not succeed because the landlord had not supplied any safety devices in the first place.The property owner also sought permission to amend his legal response to bring a counterclaim seeking common-law indemnification from Irwin. In effect, he wanted to recover compensation from the injured worker for the liability imposed on him.The appeals court rejected that request, finding that the proposed counterclaim lacked legal merit.The judges said allowing a property owner to recover damages from an injured worker on the basis of that worker's alleged negligence would undermine the purpose of Section 240(1), which provides special protection to people working at elevated locations.The decision also referred to earlier cases establishing that a worker's contributory negligence cannot be used as a defence against liability under the provision.The court unanimously affirmed the lower court's September 18 last year order, which had granted Irwin partial summary judgment on liability and rejected the landlord's request to pursue an indemnification claim.
Article Summary: Benjamin E. Irwin was cleaning vinyl siding on a rental building when he fell from its roof. He was not using any safety equipment at the time of the accident. The landlord challenged the liability ruling, arguing that the work amounted to routine maintenance and therefore did not qualify for protection.

Article Title: A Brooklyn woman discovers that her neighbour has attached a white fence to her house using screws and hardware while occupying a three-foot strip of her land; the court orders the fence removed as th
Article Text:
Representative image

How a white fence became the centre of a property dispute

Screws allegedly compromised the house's exterior protection

Neighbouring property sale raises urgency of the dispute

Woman approaches court without a lawyer

Judge orders fence removed and disputed strip excluded from sale

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Final ownership and damages remain to be decided

A Brooklyn homeowner has secured a court order against her neighbours after alleging that they attached a white fence directly to her house using screws and other hardware while occupying a three-foot-wide strip of her property. Lorena Volokhova, who owns a house on Lake Avenue in Brooklyn, New York, claimed that the adjoining property owners had extended their occupation beyond their boundary and caused damage to her home's exterior. The dispute became more urgent when the neighbours began preparing to sell their property, allegedly including the contested strip in the sale. Volokhova approached the court seeking intervention, and on July 10, 2026, a judge granted a preliminary injunction directing the neighbours to remove the fence and stop occupying the disputed land.The case involves two adjoining properties at 14A and 15A Lake Avenue in Brooklyn. Volokhova owns the house at 14A, while Hanardi Corp. is the registered owner of the neighbouring property at 15A. Khanna Nazarova was named as an individual defendant and identified in the proceedings as the corporation's principal, owner, officer and/or authorised representative.According to Volokhova's complaint, the neighbours occupied a three-foot-wide strip of land between the two houses, which she maintained was part of her property.She also alleged that they attached a white fence to the exterior of her house using screws, fasteners and other hardware.Volokhova argued that the fence was not simply positioned along the boundary but was physically fixed to her building, effectively allowing the neighbours to exercise control over the disputed strip.Volokhova told the court that attaching the fence to her house had created openings and penetrations in its exterior. She alleged that these damaged the building's waterproofing, weatherproofing and protective systems, leaving it vulnerable to water intrusion and further deterioration.She maintained that the longer the fence remained attached, the greater the potential damage to her property. Her complaint included claims involving trespass, encroachment, property boundaries, quiet title, permanent injunctive relief and property damage.The disagreement took on added significance when Hanardi Corp. and Nazarova were reportedly preparing to sell the property at 15A Lake Avenue. Volokhova feared that the three-foot strip would be included in the proposed sale, potentially creating further complications if a new owner acquired the adjoining property.She also raised concerns that photographs used on real estate listing websites could give prospective buyers the impression that the disputed strip and the fence attached to her house were part of the property being offered for sale.To support her claim, Volokhova submitted two property surveys, one dating from 2004 and another dated March 31, 2026. She argued that both showed the disputed strip fell within the boundaries of her property.Volokhova filed the case without legal representation and sought an urgent order requiring the neighbours to detach and remove the fence. She also asked the court to recognise her ownership of the disputed strip and prevent the neighbouring property from being sold with the contested area included.The defendants did not file opposition to her application for a preliminary injunction. The court considered her application, supporting affidavits, property surveys and other submitted documents before deciding whether interim protection was necessary.On July 10, 2026, New York Supreme Court Justice Aaron D. Maslow, sitting in Kings County, granted Volokhova's application for a preliminary injunction in Volokhova v. Hanardi Corp., Index No. 608/2026.The judge found that the two surveys supported her claim that the fence and the occupied strip were on her property. The court also concluded that she had demonstrated a likelihood of success in the case, the possibility of irreparable harm and that the balance of equities favoured granting interim relief.The order directed Hanardi Corp. and Nazarova to remove the white fence attached to Volokhova's house and stop occupying the three-foot-wide strip. They were also required to remove any property they had placed there. In addition, advertisements for the sale of 15A Lake Avenue were prohibited from representing the disputed strip or the fence as part of the property being offered.The judge required Volokhova to deposit an undertaking of $2,500 with the County Clerk as security connected with the preliminary injunction.The July 10 order provided interim protection to Volokhova, but it did not conclude the entire legal dispute. The judge left the question of a final declaration of ownership, permanent relief and any compensation for property damage for a later determination.The court also noted that the defendants had not yet answered the amended complaint and that Volokhova had not sought a default judgment. The ruling therefore addressed the immediate encroachment and the proposed property sale while the underlying case remained unresolved.
Article Summary: Judge orders fence removed and disputed strip excluded from sale. Dispute became more urgent when neighbours began preparing to sell their property, allegedly including the contested strip in the sale. Lorena Volokhova claims neighbours extended their occupation beyond their boundary and caused damage to her home's exterior.

Article Title: California prepares for flooding, heavy rain and strong winds before Thanksgiving as king tides and mountain snow threaten holiday travel across the West Coast
Article Text:
Image: Canva

California faces heavy rain, flooding and strong winds during Thanksgiving week

King tides could worsen coastal flooding across San Francisco Bay

A view of flooding on the Embarcadero amid heavy rainfall in San Francisco, California, on November 18, 2026. (Image: Tayfun Coskun)

Thanksgiving travel faces possible road closures and dangerous conditions

Northern and Southern California could both see coastal flooding

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

California is preparing for another round of heavy rain, flooding and strong winds as storms move towards the state during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. A Pacific storm is expected to reach Northern California on Tuesday and Wednesday, bringing an atmospheric river, persistent rainfall and potentially hazardous travel conditions. The threat comes at the same time as the year's highest tides, raising the risk of coastal flooding across the San Francisco Bay Area. Officials have moved emergency resources into position, while forecasters warn that rain, wind, snow and high surf could complicate Thanksgiving travel.The latest storm system is expected to reach the Northern California coast on Tuesday and Wednesday, bringing moisture from the Pacific in the form of an atmospheric river. According to NBC News, the National Weather Service's San Francisco Bay Area office forecast widespread and persistent rain, with up to 3 inches possible in northern parts of the region.The rain is expected to arrive alongside strong winds. Gusts of up to 45 mph are possible in parts of the Bay Area, while the combination of heavy rainfall, runoff and high tides could increase the risk of flooding in low-lying areas.A coastal flood warning covering the Bay Area coastline is in effect from Monday morning through Thursday afternoon, with nearly 3 feet of inundation possible in vulnerable locations.The weather threat is not limited to rainfall. The first storm is expected to bring fresh snow to higher elevations of the Sierra Nevada, potentially creating difficult driving conditions during the Thanksgiving travel rush. The National Weather Service office in Reno warned that the snow could produce periods of difficult travel during an already busy holiday period.A second storm containing atmospheric river precipitation is also expected to follow the first system. Forecasters said there was considerable uncertainty about the second storm's exact timing, location and strength, with another round of unsettled weather potentially arriving later in the week.The storm threat is particularly concerning because it coincides with king tides, the highest tides of the year. The California Coastal Commission said the king tides are expected from Tuesday through Thursday, meaning heavy rain and storm runoff could reach waterways at the same time as exceptionally high tides.The ABC News report said the National Weather Service warned that high tides could cause flooding of low-lying infrastructure, road closures and coastal erosion. Wednesday morning's high tide could approach the highest level on record in San Francisco, with the full moon, elevated surf and El Niño conditions contributing to unusually high water levels.King tides across the Bay Area could reach 7.5 to 8 feet above the average low tide, according to the US Coast Guard. Water levels could rise 1 to 2 feet above normal high tides and potentially higher if the peak tides coincide with an incoming storm. Coastal and low-lying areas around San Francisco Bay, San Pablo Bay, Marin County, San Mateo County and the San Francisco waterfront are among the areas vulnerable to temporary flooding and closures.The combination of storm runoff and high tides has already prompted preparations in San Francisco. Mayor Daniel Lurie said the city's emergency operations centre was being activated ahead of the expected rain and tide-driven flooding. He also urged residents to consider staying home rather than travelling during the most hazardous part of the week.The timing of the storms could make the weather particularly disruptive because Tuesday and Wednesday are expected to be among the busiest road travel days before Thanksgiving. Heavy rain, coastal flooding, strong winds and mountain snow could affect roads at the same time as millions of people begin travelling for the holiday.According to ABC News, AAA estimates that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday and the following Monday. The weather threat therefore comes during a period when California roads and airports are expected to be under heavy demand.The California Governor's Office of Emergency Services has moved resources, including swift-water rescue teams, to areas where they may be needed because of the potential for heavy rainfall and flooding. The state is preparing for the possibility that rising water could affect roads and other infrastructure during the holiday period.Some transportation precautions have already been announced. California Department of Transportation officials said the Posey Tube, an East Bay tunnel connecting Alameda Island with Oakland beneath the Oakland Estuary, would be closed as a precaution from Sunday through Friday. Other coastal roads and low-lying routes could also face temporary closures if flooding develops.Northern California is expected to experience the strongest impacts from the first storm, but coastal flooding concerns extend farther south. The National Weather Service has issued a coastal flood advisory covering parts of the Southern California coast, including Catalina and Santa Barbara islands and sections of Santa Barbara County.ABC News reported that the first storm was expected to bring lighter rain to San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties, while significant rainfall was less likely to reach urban Los Angeles. Even so, high tides and elevated surf could create flooding concerns along exposed coastal areas.The Port of San Diego also planned to close two public-access trails along San Diego Bay for the week because of king tide concerns. The precautions reflect a broader West Coast threat, with coastal flood alerts and high-surf advisories covering large sections of the Pacific coastline.The unsettled pattern is expected to continue beyond the first storm. Forecasters are tracking another system that could affect the West Coast later in the week, although its precise timing and strength remain uncertain. For California residents and Thanksgiving travellers, the combination of heavy rain, strong winds, high tides and mountain snow means conditions could change quickly during one of the country's busiest travel periods.
Article Summary: Pacific storm is expected to reach Northern California on Tuesday and Wednesday, bringing persistent rainfall and strong winds. Storm comes at the same time as the year's highest tides, raising the risk of coastal flooding across the San Francisco Bay Area. Officials have moved emergency resources into position, while forecasters warn that rain, wind, snow and high surf could complicate Thanksgiving travel.

Fake ICE uniforms were used to scare Latino tenants into leaving. Representational photo

Tenants challenged property management

Emails and messages presented during trial

Other tenants settled, but Elrods continued lawsuit

A Los Angeles couple have been awarded $7.65 million after winning a legal battle against the company that owned their former apartment building in Koreatown. The case involved allegations that the landlord used intimidation, rent increases and poor living conditions to push residents out of their homes.Andrew and Brigid Elrod took legal action against K3 Holdings after becoming involved in efforts to organise tenants living in the building. According to LA Times, they alleged that the company retaliated against residents who challenged its practices and wanted tenants paying lower rents to leave so that the apartments could be rented at higher rates.The case took a significant turn during the trial when a former employee of K3 Holdings gave evidence about a suggestion allegedly made by the company's principal, Nathan Kadisha. According to the former asset manager, Kadisha had proposed that employees wear fake Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) uniforms to frighten Latino tenants into leaving a building. The former employee also testified that Kadisha did not want African Americans to rent the company's properties.The jury ultimately found the landlord responsible for harassing and retaliating against the Elrods. It also found that the company had failed to maintain the apartment building properly.The couple received $4.5 million for the impact of their experience, including anxiety, humiliation, grief, inconvenience and emotional distress. A further $3.15 million was awarded as punitive damages against K3 Holdings and three related companies.The decision was delivered on Friday by a Los Angeles Superior Court jury. It was an 11-1 verdict, bringing the couple's case to a successful conclusion after they chose to continue with the lawsuit while several other tenants reached settlements.The Elrods' involvement in the dispute dates back to 2021, when a limited liability corporation controlled by K3 Holdings purchased their apartment building at 974 S. Gramercy Place in Koreatown.After the acquisition, the couple joined other residents in setting up a tenants' association. They also became active in the K3 Tenant Council, which was affiliated with the Los Angeles Tenants Union.Their organising activities were followed by a confrontation with the landlord over construction work at the property. The residents raised concerns about what they described as illegal and unsafe construction practices. The Elrods later took part in a sit-in protest against the work.Rose Lenehan, an organiser with the Tenants Union, said the couple were served eviction notices after participating in the protest. They continued to face eviction threats and eventually left the apartment in 2023.The couple alleged that these actions were part of a wider effort to remove tenants who were paying rents below the prevailing market rates. According to their claims, K3 Holdings used maintenance problems, construction activities and intimidation to encourage residents to accept buyout offers and vacate their homes.The company's property portfolio included 39 buildings. However, the jury's verdict in the Elrods' case concerned only the Koreatown property.The jury also considered communications involving Kadisha during the proceedings. These included text messages and emails that formed part of the evidence against the property company.One message discussed how construction-related displacement could help the company persuade tenants to accept financial offers to leave.In the message, Kadisha told a colleague that forcing tenants to relocate during construction would "be a very strong case to take the buyout", according to a statement on the verdict issued by the Los Angeles Tenants Union.The jury examined the company's treatment of residents in detail. Its 30-page verdict included findings on several questions relating to the landlord's conduct.It found that K3 Holdings and its subsidiaries had raised rents and reduced utility services as ways of putting pressure on tenants to move out. The jury also concluded that the companies had engaged in conduct covered by Los Angeles' 2021 Tenant Anti-Harassment Ordinance.Jacob Woocher, one of the lawyers representing the Elrods, said the evidence was not limited to the couple's individual experience.He said the trial had presented material about the company's practices across several properties, even though the verdict itself covered only the building where the couple had lived.The Elrods were among several tenants involved in a 2022 lawsuit against K3 Holdings. According to Lenehan, a number of the other residents eventually settled their claims.The couple decided to continue pursuing their case instead. Their legal team included the Los Angeles Center for Community Law and Action and Alfredo Nava of the Law Office of Alfredo Nava.Their decision meant that the allegations were examined in a trial, where the jury heard testimony from a former company employee and considered internal communications and other evidence.The final award included both compensation for the harm suffered by the couple and punitive damages against the companies. The $4.5 million in non-economic damages covered the past and future impact of the alleged harassment, while the additional $3.15 million was imposed as punishment.
Article Summary: Andrew and Brigid Elrod took legal action against K3 Holdings after becoming involved in efforts to organise tenants living in the building. They alleged that the company retaliated against residents who challenged its practices and wanted tenants paying lower rents to leave so that the apartments could be rented at higher rates. The jury ultimately found the landlord responsible for harassing and retaliating against the Elrods.

Article Title: David and Louise Matchett exchanged more than 1,400 letters while he served overseas in World War II; their daughter later gave the collection to a local historical society
Article Text:
AI Representation: David and Louise Matchett exchanged more than 1,400 letters while he served overseas in World War II. Image credits: Chatgpt

A marriage interrupted by military service

How

V-Mail

helped them stay connected

A sample image of a V-Mail envelope. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

‘Prince’ and ‘Snow White’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The letter became part of a

historical collection

During World War II, many individuals were separated from loved ones due to the deployment of soldiers to overseas territories. Writing letters became one of the ways through which individuals could share news and exchange affection with each other. For newlyweds, David and Louise Matchett, these letters became a vital component in their marital life. The couple’s correspondence started in 1942 and went on through most of the war period to capture their thoughts and experiences of the separation. David and Louise had both been raised in the South Side of Chicago. David had been working as a practicing lawyer while Louise had started her bachelor’s degree at the University of Chicago before they got married in 1942. Within three weeks after getting married, David had enlisted for military service at Fort Sheridan, Illinois. Most of the war period, he spent time overseas while Louise stayed in the United States. From July 1942 through October 1944, the couple exchanged more than 1,400 letters. This communication ultimately formed a private account of their marriage and daily activities during World War II. Their daughter, Mary Kingery and husband, Daniel, donated this collection to the Winnetka Historical Society many years later. The Winnetka Historical Society wrote about this love story in its Spring 2011 Gazette under the heading “Matchett Letters Open Door on WWII Love Story,” written by Susan Crowe Whitcomb.Both David and Louise grew up on the South Side of Chicago. They were children of influential people in the city. David’s father was a judge on the Cook County Appellate Court, while Louise’s father was the principal of Fenger High School. The Gazette says that when they married in 1942, David was a practicing attorney and Louise was finishing her bachelor's degree at the University of Chicago. Soon after the couple's marriage, David left for his military service at Fort Sheridan.According to the Gazette, David was attached to the Army Medical Corps for most of the war, much of it in Papua, New Guinea. While he did not fight himself, David saw the impact of the war on injured soldiers who came to the hospital where he was stationed. The earlier letters were filled with the reasons why he thought the US was at war. Later, military regulations prevented him from disclosing details about his location and movements to Louise in case the letters were to fall into the wrong hands. In a letter to Louise dated January 19 44, David explained that he could not say where he was and where he was going to go because even he did not know that. These restrictions left her with limited information about his surroundings, but their correspondence continued.Letters were an important part of communication between military personnel and their families during World War II. The Winnetka Historical Society’s account explains that correspondence helped maintain morale among soldiers overseas and encouraged support for the effort at home. According to the Gazette, the Matchetts were fond of using V-Mails, which were introduced in 1942 through collaboration of the US Post Office and the War and Navy Departments. V-Mails were meant to minimise the amount of space required to ship large amounts of overseas mail.The messages were written on the sheets of paper provided by the Post Office. The letters were taken to the processing centre, where they were opened, censored and photographed on microfilm. This film was shipped overseas, where the messages were printed and delivered to their destinations. The Matchetts made use of this service frequently. Louise wrote almost daily, filling her V-Mail sheets with stories about what was going on at home and talk of their future life together. Their letters talked about their friends who died during the war or were shot down while fighting above enemy lines.While there were instances when David was asked about his military duties and his views on various news reports, their love towards one another constituted the main focus of their correspondence. For instance, Louise always called David her ‘Prince,’ and he used to call her ‘Snow White’. The couple sent each other messages about their life together, expectations for the future and dreams of the day when they would reunite. In one of their letters written in March 1944, Louise assured David that he was still the most important man in her life. Moreover, she stated that she always prayed for his good health and success, and wished that he would return as quickly as possible. He responded to her in the same way. In one of the letters sent in the same month, David stated that seeing Louise after disembarkation in the United States would be the happiest event after their wedding. At the end of his letter, he told Louise that he loved her with all his heart and nothing could ever come between them.David came back to the United States during late 1944 for Judge Advocate General Officer Candidate School in Ann Arbor, Michigan. He continued his career in the JAG Corps up until 1946. In the 1950s, David and Louise moved from Chicago to Northfield, Illinois and lived there along with their daughter, Mary. David died in 1974, whereas Louise died in 2011. Their daughter, Mary Kingery and her husband, Daniel, donated the letters to the Winnetka Historical Society. The collection consisted of over 1,400 letters that were written from July 1942 to October 1944. The historical society’s account of the collection offers a personal view of World War II, beyond military records and official reports. The letters document the restrictions placed on overseas correspondence, the role of V-Mail and the everyday concerns of a couple separated by military service. What started as a way for two newlyweds to stay connected became an invaluable historical document. In the words of Louise and David themselves, future generations will get to know their story, their aspirations and the fears of living in the midst of a worldwide war.
Article Summary: David and Louise Matchett exchanged more than 1,400 letters while he served overseas in World War II. The couple’s correspondence started in 1942 and went on through most of the war period to capture their thoughts and experiences of the separation. Their daughter, Mary Kingery and husband, Daniel, donated this collection to the Winnetka Historical Society.

Article Title: Snowflake billionaire Frank Slootman and wife Brenda give $1,000 each to 22,081 Montana children who missed Trump's federal seed money; the donation will give them an early financial head start throug
Article Text:
Why are these children receiving $1,000 from the billionaire couple?

How will the $1,000 contributions work?

Who are Frank and Brenda Slootman?

Other billionaires are also funding Trump Accounts

What the donation means for Montana families

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Billionaire technology executive Frank Slootman and his wife Brenda have committed $22.081 million to provide $1,000 each to 22,081 children across Montana through the Trump Accounts programme. The donation targets children born in 2023 and 2024, who fall outside the birth-year eligibility window for the US government's separate $1,000 seed contribution. Announced by the US Department of the Treasury on November 19, 2026, the contribution is being made through the Slootman Family Foundation. According to the foundation, the money has already been deposited and invested in the children's accounts. The initiative aims to give these children an early financial asset that can potentially grow through long-term investments before they reach adulthood.The donation is aimed at a specific group of children who do not qualify for the federal government's initial $1,000 contribution under the Trump Accounts programme.Under the federal scheme, eligible US citizen children born between January 1, 2025, and December 31, 2028, with valid Social Security numbers can receive a one-time $1,000 contribution from the US Treasury Department. However, parents or guardians must submit the required election to claim this contribution, even if an account has already been opened automatically.Children born in 2023 and 2024 fall outside this particular federal seed-money window. However, they are not excluded from holding Trump Accounts. Eligible children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers can have accounts even if they do not qualify for the government's initial contribution.The Slootman Family Foundation has stepped in to provide the same $1,000 starting contribution to 22,081 children born during those two years in Montana. The total commitment amounts to $22,081,000.According to the foundation's announcement, the contributions have already been deposited through the Treasury Department and invested in the children's accounts.The money is being deposited into Trump Accounts, which are tax-advantaged investment accounts created for eligible American children under the Working Families Tax Cuts legislation signed into law in 2025.Unlike ordinary savings accounts, these accounts are designed to hold investments that can potentially grow over an extended period. During childhood, funds are generally invested in eligible low-cost mutual funds or exchange-traded funds tracking broad US stock-market indices.Parents or guardians must claim and activate their children's accounts before they can manage them. Once an account is claimed, family members and friends can contribute towards the investment, subject to an annual combined limit of $5,000 for ordinary individual and employer contributions.Employers can contribute up to $2,500 annually towards an employee's Trump Account or that of an eligible dependent. However, this amount counts towards the same $5,000 annual limit rather than being an additional allowance. Certain government and charitable contributions are governed by separate rules and may fall outside this limit.The money is intended to remain invested for the long term. When the beneficiary reaches adulthood, the account generally becomes subject to traditional individual retirement account rules, including applicable tax and withdrawal restrictions.The accounts are not restricted to college expenses, unlike conventional education savings plans. Instead, they are designed to provide children with a financial asset that can continue growing beyond their school years.Frank Slootman is a Dutch-born American technology executive and billionaire investor known for leading several major software companies.He previously served as chief executive of Data Domain, where he led the company through its public listing in 2007 before its acquisition by EMC in 2009. He subsequently became president and CEO of ServiceNow in 2011, overseeing its growth and 2012 stock market listing.In 2019, Slootman joined cloud-data company Snowflake as its CEO and led it through its September 2020 public listing. He stepped down from the chief executive position in February 2024 but continued as chairman of the company's board. Snowflake's current CEO is Sridhar Ramaswamy.Forbes estimated his net worth at approximately $3.5 billion in November 2026. His wealth has largely been built through his leadership roles in the technology and enterprise software industries.His wife Brenda is also named as a donor in the Treasury Department's announcement. The couple are based in Bozeman, Montana, and are making the contribution through their Slootman Family Foundation.The Slootmans are among several wealthy individuals and families contributing to the Trump Accounts programme through private donations.Michael and Susan Dell previously pledged $6.25 billion to provide $250 contributions to approximately 25 million eligible American children born before 2025. Their initiative focuses on children aged 10 and younger living in qualifying ZIP codes with median household incomes below $150,000.According to the Slootman Family Foundation's announcement, another 118,523 Montana children qualify for the Dell family's $250 contribution, subject to the initiative's eligibility requirements.This means some children born in 2023 and 2024 could potentially benefit from both initiatives, receiving the Slootmans' $1,000 contribution as well as the separate $250 Dell contribution if they meet the relevant conditions.Investor Ray Dalio and his wife Barbara have also pledged $75 million to support contributions for eligible children in Connecticut, particularly those from lower-income households.These contributions are separate from the federal government's own $1,000 seed-money initiative. They demonstrate how private donors can use the account system to extend investment opportunities to children who may not qualify for the initial government contribution.The contribution provides thousands of Montana families with an opportunity to begin building investment savings for their children from an early age.The Slootman Family Foundation's commitment covers 22,081 children born in 2023 and 2024 across the state, providing each with an initial $1,000 investment contribution.Montana Governor Greg Gianforte welcomed the donation, thanking the Slootman family for supporting investment accounts for children across the state. He also encouraged families to activate their children's accounts and explore the investment opportunities available through the federal programme.The foundation has encouraged parents and relatives to consider making additional contributions on birthdays, holidays and other occasions.For the children covered by the donation, the $1,000 contribution provides an investment starting point that could remain invested for many years before they reach adulthood. The eventual value will depend on investment performance and applicable account rules.
Article Summary: Frank Slootman and his wife Brenda have committed $22.081 million to provide $1,000 each to 22,081 children across Montana through the Trump Accounts programme. The donation targets children born in 2023 and 2024, who fall outside the birth-year eligibility window for the US government's separate $ 1,000 seed contribution. The money is being deposited into Trump Accounts, which are tax- advantaged investment accounts created for eligible American children.

Blueberry Hill

Ain’t That a Shame

Blue Monday

Katrina left Domino’s home and music collection damaged

FEMA urban search-and-rescue personnel assist residents in flooded New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina on August 31, 2005. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

During Hurricane Katrina, which hit New Orleans on August 29, 2005, Fats Domino, one of the greatest rock ‘n’ roll artists, stayed in his house located in the Lower Ninth Ward of New Orleans. He became unreachable as water flooded his area when he was 77 years old. His relatives and manager thought that he was lost until a picture of him from a rescue boat appeared. Born Antoine Domino, he lived in the same neighbourhood where he grew up from the beginning of the 1960s. He was famous for such songs as “”, “” and “”.Domino's longtime agent, Al Embry, called him on the Sunday before the hurricane struck and tried to persuade him to evacuate. Embry told Reuters that Domino insisted he was going to "try to ride out" the storm at home. When the floodwaters came into the area, Embry could no longer get hold of him. Enquiries from officials within the city and the state did not aid in finding him.Karen Domino White, Domino's daughter, spotted her father in a photo published in The Times-Picayune, the first sign that he had survived.This photo was captured on the night of August 29 and portrayed a man who was helped off a boat by some rescuers. The September 2 Los Angeles Times article says that although the photo suggested he had survived, she still did not know where her father had been taken. The Associated Press later confirmed in a May 2007 report that Domino was rescued by boat from his flooded Ninth Ward home after the storm struck on August 29, 2005. CBS News reported that relatives spent four tense days waiting for news before the rescue-boat photograph gave them the first sign he was safe.Domino was able to make it back to his Ninth Ward residence to assess the damage done. In March 2007, according to the Associated Press, Domino walked around his devastated property as the workers began working on the reconstruction of his home, which had been damaged by the floods.The hurricane also took a heavy toll on his musical belongings. May 20, 2007, Los Angeles Times report, published after his first public performance since Katrina, Domino said he had lost his home, pianos, gold and platinum records and much of the city he loved. Eventually, the musician came back on stage in New Orleans in May 2007.Domino’s story is just one of the many individual accounts that emerged because of Hurricane Katrina. This hurricane destroyed New Orleans, wrecked countless homes and made people all over the city leave their homes to look for refuge elsewhere. The ability of Domino’s to survive the rising waters was crucial because he could come back to the neighbourhood where he spent most of his life and, at the same time, marked the moment of his return to the stage and May 2007. The performer will remain strongly linked to New Orleans, the city where he lived and which influenced his music and career.
Article Summary: Fats Domino, one of the greatest rock ‘n’ roll artists, stayed in his house located in the Lower Ninth Ward of New Orleans. He became unreachable as water flooded his area when he was 77 years old. His relatives and manager thought that he was lost until a picture of him from a rescue boat appeared.

Article Title: In 1969, film critic Rex Reed bought an apartment in New York’s famous Dakota building for just $30,000; after nearly 60 years, the two-bedroom home is listed for $5.99 million to support his foundati
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A Manhattan apartment that witnessed nearly six decades of Hollywood history is now on the property market, carrying an asking price of $5.99 million. The former home of late film critic and journalist Rex Reed, located inside New York City’s celebrated Dakota building, is being offered for $5,999,000, with proceeds from the sale and an accompanying estate auction set to support the Rex Reed Foundation. Realtor dot com first reported the listing, while 6sqft and Robb Report have also highlighted the property’s connection to the veteran film critic. Reed purchased the two-bedroom apartment in 1969 for $30,000 and remained there until his death on May 12, 2026, at the age of 87. According to the Associated Press, he spent more than six decades as a prominent voice in American film and cultural criticism, writing for publications including The New York Times, Vogue, Esquire and The New York Observer.The apartment, identified as Residence 86, occupies a high floor of the Dakota at 1 West 72nd Street on Manhattan’s Upper West Side. Spanning approximately 2,000 square feet, the two-bedroom, two-bathroom residence retains its original pre-war layout, with a formal entrance gallery, a large living room and a separate dining room. The property was listed on November 13 through Sotheby’s International Realty.Its interiors reflect the character of a home accumulated over decades rather than a recently designed luxury residence.The apartment features high ceilings, oak flooring, Regency-style doors and crown mouldings, alongside north- and west-facing windows that offer views across the surrounding cityscape. The formal dining room also includes a pantry and dry bar, while both bedrooms have en-suite bathrooms and generous closet space.Reed used the second bedroom as his office, where built-in shelves accommodated his extensive collection of books and films. The apartment also served as a gathering place for personalities from the entertainment world. Over the years, Reed hosted guests including Lauren Bacall, Boris Karloff and Truman Capote, making the residence part of New York’s wider cultural history.The building itself adds considerably to the property’s appeal. Completed in 1884 and designed by architect Henry J. Hardenbergh, who also designed the Plaza Hotel, the Dakota is regarded as one of Manhattan’s most recognisable residential landmarks. Its distinctive architecture, featuring elaborate gables, arches and ornate detailing, has made it a fixture of Central Park West. The building also gained wider recognition through its association with notable residents, including John Lennon.According to the property listing, the Dakota offers residents a gated entrance, a landscaped central courtyard with restored fountains, concierge services, a resident manager and a fitness centre. Monthly maintenance for the apartment is listed at $8,842. The building permits pets and pieds-à-terre, while buyers can finance up to 50 per cent of the purchase price.The sale is also accompanied by an auction of Reed’s personal collection. Auction house Doyle organised a November 23 sale featuring furniture, artwork, books, decorations and memorabilia from his Dakota residence, offering collectors an opportunity to acquire pieces associated with the critic’s private life.The proceeds from the apartment sale and the estate auction are intended to benefit the Rex Reed Foundation, established to honour his legacy and support storytelling and cultural initiatives. The foundation’s website describes its mission as recognising Reed’s contribution to American cultural criticism and preserving his influence across film, theatre, literature and entertainment. The listing marks the end of a remarkable chapter for an apartment that remained Reed’s home through changing eras of New York life. What began as a $30,000 purchase in 1969 is now a nearly $6 million property, with its next sale expected to carry forward the legacy of the man who called it home for almost six decades.
Article Summary: The two-bedroom, two-bathroom residence is located inside New York City’s celebrated Dakota building. Reed purchased the apartment in 1969 for $30,000 and remained there until his death on May 12, 2026, at the age of 87. Over the years, Reed hosted guests including Lauren Bacall, Boris Karloff and Truman Capote.

Article Title: LeT, JeM proxies exposed, ISI eyes revival of 19 dormant terror outfits in Jammu and Kashmir
Article Text:
How ISI plans to rebuild terror networks in J&K

19 dormant terror outfits on ISI radar

Local recruitment, infiltration among key concerns

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence ( ISI ) is exploring a shift in its strategy in Jammu and Kashmir , with plans to bring back dormant terror outfits in the Valley as its existing proxy groups face increased scrutiny from the security agencies, news agency IANS reported.Pakistan's ugly motive is to create a network of revived terror outfits that can operate without any apparent links to established Pakistan-based organisations such as the Lashkar-e-Taiba ( LeT ) and Jaish-e-Mohammed ( JeM ), according to officials cited by IANS.The Hafiz Saeed-led LeT has been operating through The Resistance Front (TRF), while Masood Azhar's JeM has been linked to proxy outfits such as the People's Anti-Fascist Front (PAFF), Kashmir Tigers (KT) and Lashkar-e-Mustafa.However, investigations by agencies such as the Jammu and Kashmir Police and the National Investigation Agency (NIA) have increasingly exposed the links between these outfits and their parent organisations. The agencies have gathered evidence indicating that the different names are being used to mask the involvement of the LeT and JeM.An official told IANS that the ISI has now advised these groups to reconnect with former members of terror organisations that have been inactive in Jammu and Kashmir for years.Several of these outfits emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when militancy was at its peak in the Valley. However, as the ISI concentrated its operations around the LeT, JeM and Hizbul Mujahideen, many smaller groups gradually became inactive.Some ran out of funds, while others lost their operatives to security force operations, the official said.According to data cited by IANS, Jammu and Kashmir currently has 10 active terror groups, while 19 outfits remain inactive. Among the dormant organisations are the Kashmir Jehad Force (KJF) and Tehrik-e-Jihad (TeJ).An Intelligence Bureau official said the ISI is likely to focus on locating former members of these groups and encouraging them to rebuild their networks."These members would be told to look out for potential recruits and then revive these terror groups. There would be no direct link between these groups and the existing terror outfits. This helps the ISI in covering its tracks when an investigation into a terror attack is launched," the official said.A major consideration behind the proposed strategy is that several of these organisations are homegrown rather than Pakistan-based. Their revival could make it more difficult for investigators to establish direct links with established terror outfits operating from across the border, the report said.The ISI is also expected to draw on the experience of former members in areas such as recruitment and logistics. Although many of them are now older, officials believe their knowledge of local networks could prove useful in rebuilding the outfits.The agency is likely to focus on recruiting local youth, while Pakistan continues to explore ways to increase infiltration into Jammu and Kashmir through multiple routes, an official told IANS.Another official said the ISI is keen to restore militant activity in the Valley. However, the recent killing of Lashkar commander Lateef Bhat has dealt a setback to its plans and could delay efforts to revive terror networks for some time.The revived groups could be used for both ground operations and information warfare, including disinformation and propaganda campaigns, officials said.This would require security agencies to tackle not only possible terror operations but also coordinated attempts to influence public opinion through propaganda, adding to the security challenges in Jammu and Kashmir, the report said.
Article Summary: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence ( ISI ) is exploring a shift in its strategy in Jammu and Kashmir. It plans to bring back dormant terror outfits in the Valley as its existing proxy groups face increased scrutiny. The revived groups could be used for both ground operations and information warfare, including disinformation and propaganda campaigns.

Article Title: Pakistan petrol pumps threaten nationwide shutdown, give govt 15 days to meet demands
Article Text:
Pakistan's fuel crisis fears grow as petrol dealers threaten nationwide shutdown

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan's petroleum dealers have threatened to shut down petrol pumps across the country if the government fails to introduce a monthly fuel pricing mechanism, giving authorities 15 days to address their demands, according to a report by Dawn.The Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) said frequent revisions in petroleum prices were causing serious financial difficulties for fuel retailers and rapidly depleting their working capital. The association warned that continued uncertainty could force petrol pumps to suspend operations, potentially triggering a law and order situation.Addressing a presser at the Karachi Press Club, PPDA chairman Malik Khuda Bakhsh, along with other association representatives, demanded that dealers' profit margins be raised to 8 per cent of the retail price. They also alleged that refineries had cut petrol and diesel supplies, with one refinery reportedly halting diesel supplies altogether, Dawn reported.The dealers claimed that they collectively contribute PKR 5.74 billion to the national exchequer every day and urged the government to take their financial concerns into account before introducing further changes to petroleum-related policies.Khuda Bakhsh said previous strike threats had been withdrawn following government intervention, but several demands remained unresolved.He argued that changing market conditions following the US-Iran war made it necessary for the authorities to reconsider the existing pricing arrangement, according to Dawn.Pakistan introduced the daily fuel pricing mechanism in July, citing volatility in international oil markets. Under the system, the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) announces revised petroleum prices every day.The PPDA has repeatedly opposed the arrangement, demanding a return to monthly or fortnightly price revisions. Earlier, another petroleum dealers' association had also postponed its nationwide strike following assurances from the petroleum minister that the daily pricing system would initially operate on a trial basis.In August, the government approved a 15.5 per cent increase in dealers' margins on petrol and high-speed diesel. The move raised the margin by PKR 1.34 per litre to PKR 9.98, effective September 1. However, the dealers' demand for an 8 per cent margin remains unresolved.
Article Summary: Pakistan's petroleum dealers have threatened to shut down petrol pumps across the country if the government fails to introduce a monthly fuel pricing mechanism. The Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association said frequent revisions in petroleum prices were causing serious financial difficulties for fuel retailers. The association warned that continued uncertainty could force petrol pumps to suspend operations.

Article Title: SCO: Pakistan set to invite India for culture ministers' meeting
Article Text:
The only significant visit to Pakistan from India after the April 2025 Pahalgam attack was by MEA additional secretary Alok Dimri for a meeting of the SCO national coordinators in September

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

After participating in the SCO inaugural civilisational dialogue in New Delhi, Pakistan is now all set to deliver an invitation to India for a meeting of the culture ministers it will host under its presidency of the Eurasian bloc early next year. It will be interesting to see how India responds as no Indian minister has visited Pakistan since the Pahalgam terrorist attack.Significantly, Islamabad is also preparing to host the SCO heads of state council summit - where India is usually represented by PM Narendra Modi -next year in late August, after initially considering having it on August 14 – Pakistan's Independence Day. An August 14 summit is unlikely to have seen participation by India at any level.The only significant visit to Pakistan from India after the April 2025 Pahalgam attack was by MEA additional secretary Alok Dimri for a meeting of the SCO national coordinators in September – shortly after Pakistan assumed presidency – to firm up the calendar of events under Islamabad's stewardship.After what is officially called Meeting of Ministers of Culture (SCO-MMC), Pakistan will also host more high-profile meetings of the SCO defence and foreign ministers in the run up to the Islamabad summit in August.The meeting for cultural cooperation among SCO member-states in Pakistan is a relatively low-stakes event for India that keeps political commitments minimal, unlike the foreign and defence high-level gatherings which might raise the political temperature at home.The last minister to visit Pakistan was S Jaishankar for a meeting of the SCO foreign ministers' meeting in October 2024, well before Pahalgam.Amid criticism by the Opposition for hosting Pakistan minister Musadik Malik for the Modi-proposed civilisational dialogue last week, India reiterated there was no dilution of its position on the Indus Waters Treaty that was "put in abeyance" after the Pahalgam attack. India has stressed that SCO cooperation should not be mistaken for bilateral thaw.The visit by Malik passed off smoothly without any bilateral friction as he adhered to the protocol of addressing multilateral SCO themes, rather than raising sensitive bilateral issues.While the key question remains whether Modi will travel to Islamabad for the SCO summit, Indian officials say such a visit is highly improbable at this stage. Any bilateral thaw that might result in Modi's visit requires, as far as India is concerned, a fundamental shift in Pakistan's position on cross-border terrorism.India is seeking tangible progress on its security concerns and doesn't want to create any optics of normalisation when these concerns remain unaddressed.The possibility of a senior minister, most likely Jaishankar, representing India is not ruled out. It would allow India to sustain its active engagement with the SCO, while not being seen as softening its Pakistan policy. Officials point to the fact that there's already a precedent for that. In 2024, it was Jaishankar who attended the heads of summit in Kazakhstan, filling in for the PM.
Article Summary: Pakistan is set to deliver an invitation to India for a meeting of the culture ministers it will host under its presidency of the Eurasian bloc early next year. No Indian minister has visited Pakistan since the Pahalgam terrorist attack. Islamabad is also preparing to host the SCO heads of state council summit next year in late August.

Article Title: Lahore tops global pollution ranking again as AQI crosses 500, eight Pakistan cities among worst
Article Text:
Choking under state neglect: Lahore once again ranks world’s most polluted city as AQI breaches 500

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Lahore once again ranked as the world's most polluted major city on Sunday morning, with its Air Quality Index (AQI) reaching 538, placing it in the hazardous category, according to Pakistani daily Dawn. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres, as severe smog continued to affect the province.Data from Swiss air quality monitoring platform IQAir showed Lahore at the top of the global major city ranking with an AQI of 538 between 9 am and 10 am. The reading exposed residents to severe health risks associated with hazardous air pollution.Karachi was further down the global ranking with an AQI of 180, followed by Cairo at 162.The pollution crisis extended beyond Lahore, with Kahna Nau in Lahore district recording the worst air quality in Pakistan at an AQI of 606. It was followed by Lahore at 538, Bahawalpur at 536, Sargodha at 392 and Gujranwala at 347, Dawn reported.Multan, Dera Ghazi Khan, Skardu, Faisalabad and Peshawar completed the list of the country's 10 most polluted cities.Lahore has repeatedly featured at the top of global pollution rankings in recent weeks.It recorded an AQI of 266 on Saturday evening, while the city had logged an hourly reading of 465 between 7 am and 8 am on Friday, as heavy smog affected several parts of Punjab.The continuing pollution has raised questions over the effectiveness of the Punjab administration's anti-smog measures. Lahore Traffic Police, however, has claimed that enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.Chief Traffic Officer Syed Abdul Rahim Shirazi said on Saturday that traffic personnel had issued challan tickets to 14,653 vehicles emitting smoke. Action was also taken against 10,306 vehicles transporting sand, soil and other materials without tarpaulin covers. Police penalised 31,618 unfit and dilapidated vehicles and took action against 272,760 overloaded vehicles, he added.Separately, enforcement squads from the Punjab Environment Protection and Climate Change Department conducted 84,370 inspections of brick kilns across the province between January 1 and November 18, Dawn reported earlier this week. During this period, authorities demolished 1,429 kilns, sealed 968 and registered 1,248 FIRs against violators.Between September 1 and November 18, which covers the peak smog period, the department carried out 29,999 inspections, demolished 519 kilns, sealed 494 and registered 408 FIRs. It also imposed fines worth PKR 101.45 million.The scale of Pakistan's air pollution is also reflected in long-term data. The 2025 World Air Quality Report put the country's average PM2.5 concentration at 67.3 micrograms per cubic metre, nearly 14 times the World Health Organisation's annual guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre, Dawn reported.The report also placed Pakistan among the world's most polluted countries, with an average AQI of 156.Globally, indoor and outdoor air pollution together account for an estimated 8.1 million deaths annually, making air pollution the second-leading risk factor for mortality worldwide. Outdoor particulate matter alone is responsible for an estimated 4.7 million deaths.
Article Summary: Lahore once again ranks world’s most polluted city as AQI breaches 500. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres. Lahore Traffic Police claims enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.

Article Title: 7 killed as tribal feud over forest ownership triggers gunfight in Pakistan

4 from one tribe, 3 from another killed in Pakistan forest ownership clash

Seven people were killed in a clash between two tribes over the ownership of a forest in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, news agency PTI reported, quoting police Saturday.The incident took place around 10pm local time on Thursday at Bilija forest in Battagram district, when armed members of the Gilal and Kaloch tribes confronted each other, leading to an exchange of gunfire.According to police, armed men from the Kaloch tribe took positions and opened fire, prompting retaliation from the Gilal side. Four members of the Gilal tribe and three from the Kaloch tribe were killed in the clash.The two tribes have been involved in a longstanding dispute over the ownership of Bilija forest, which has continued for several decades and claimed several lives in the past, police said.The Gilal tribe is associated with the Allai valley in Battagram district, while the Kaloch community belongs to neighbouring Kohistan district.Police said repeated efforts by the administrations of both districts to resolve the dispute and bring the communities together had failed to produce a permanent solution.The latest clash has once again raised concerns over the law and order situation in Imran Khan 's stronghold Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Article Title: 'I call for Imran Khan's release': UN rights chief flags ex-Pakistan PM's health, jail conditions
Article Text:
UN steps up pressure on Pakistan over Imran Khan's detention

Amnesty raises concerns over Khan's health

Family members' detention draws scrutiny
