Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think political tensions in Pakistan would decrease if Imran Khan is released? Yes, it could ease tensions No, tensions may continue It depends on the government's response 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

United Nations high commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk has called for the immediate release of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan , raising concerns over his reported deteriorating health and detention conditions. Turk also urged the Pakistani government and opposition to de-escalate political tensions surrounding the case.In an interview with Christiane Amanpour on CNN, Turk said Khan's release could help build confidence between the government and the opposition.“I call for Imran Khan’s release. I call for his proper treatment, and I actually call for de-escalation. We need to diffuse the political tensions that are around this case, which means that a confidence-building measure between the opposition and the government could be his immediate release,” Turk said.His remarks come amid growing international concern over the health and treatment of the 74-year-old former prime minister, who remains in detention at Adiala Jail. Earlier, Khan's son Kasim Khan appealed to the international community to intervene, accusing Pakistan's military leadership, headed by Army chief Asim Munir, of violence and repression.“Munir and his regime will not listen to reason. They kill, abduct and torture at will.It is time the world acted, before they kill my father, the rightful, democratically elected leader of Pakistan,” Kasim wrote in a post on X.Amnesty International has also called for urgent intervention, citing restrictions on Khan's access to family members, healthcare and legal representation.The organisation said Khan had not been allowed to meet his family since December 2025, apart from two meetings with his sister in August 2026. It also said he had not been permitted to speak to his sons over the telephone since March 2026.Amnesty expressed concern over his reported solitary confinement and isolation from human contact, warning that the conditions could affect his physical and mental health. It also flagged reports of severe blood pressure complications and alleged that authorities had denied him access to independent doctors despite an August Supreme Court order directing that he be taken to a private hospital.The organisation also raised concerns over the health of Khan's wife, Bushra Bibi, alleging that she had been denied adequate treatment for an eye condition that could lead to vision loss.Amnesty said the treatment of the detained couple violated Article 10 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which requires authorities to treat people deprived of their liberty with humanity and respect.The organisation also called for the release of Khan's sister Aleema Khan, who remains detained at Kot Lakhpat Prison in Lahore. It said three of his sisters were detained on September 20 and 21 in connection with a planned Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf march to Islamabad.Khan had also issued an open letter to Pakistan's top judges on November 16, seeking urgent medical treatment and implementation of court orders. He alleged that he had been held in “torturous solitary confinement for up to twenty-two hours a day” since December 20, 2025.
Article Summary: U.N. high commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk has called for the immediate release of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan. Turk also urged the Pakistani government and opposition to de-escalate political tensions surrounding the case. His remarks come amid growing international concern over the health and treatment of the 74-year-old former prime minister.

Article Title: 'Bloodshed in Karachi, Hyderabad': Why Bilawal Bhutto is opposing plan to redraw Pakistan's map
Article Text:
What is Pakistan's province-redrawing plan that has Bilawal Bhutto warning of bloodshed?

Why is Pakistan considering more provinces

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan Peoples Party chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari has strongly opposed the proposal to divide Pakistan into multiple provinces, warning against any attempt to split Sindh by force.He cautioned that such a move could trigger violence and bloodshed in Karachi and Hyderabad, Pakistan-based Geo TV reported.The proposal to redraw Pakistan's political map has reportedly found support among several leaders in the country's power corridors, including army chief Asim Munir and defence minister Khawaja Asif Speaking at an event at the Karachi Press Club, Bilawal said any forced division of the province would create social divisions and push ordinary people towards violence, Geo TV reported.“If the province is divided by force, society will be divided, it will lead to enmity, ordinary people will take up arms, and the bloodshed will not be limited to a single death,” he said.The remarks come amid discussions in Pakistan about reorganising its administrative structure by dividing its four provinces into smaller units. Reports have suggested that army chief Asim Munir is considering a plan to create 12 to 15 provinces or reorganise the country into as many as 160 smaller administrative units to address governance challenges.The proposal has gained support from some senior ministers, but faces opposition from political parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh, where the Bhutto-Zardari family and the PPP have a strong political base.Bilawal said the PPP was not opposed to creating new provinces but insisted that any such move must follow the wishes of the people and the constitutional process.“The PPP supports the creation of provinces in line with the wishes of the people, the Constitution and the law. Where we are opposing, it is over force and coercion. We do not want division through force,” he said.He also questioned suggestions that a referendum could be used to decide the issue, saying the Constitution already provided a procedure for creating new provinces.“If you are looking for an unconstitutional method, how can the PPP be with you?” he asked.Bilawal further said referendums in Pakistan's history had been used for undemocratic purposes. “It is not about a referendum, it is about intent,” he said.The proposal to increase the number of provinces from four to as many as 12 has gained momentum, with supporters arguing that smaller administrative units could improve governance and public services.Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif has backed the idea, saying the country's growing population requires smaller provinces for more efficient administration.Speaking to Geo News, Asif said Pakistan could consider creating 12 provinces, provided their boundaries were based on administrative needs rather than linguistic, ethnic or political considerations.However, the proposal faces a major political challenge, with no consensus among leading parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh.
Article Summary: Pakistan Peoples Party chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari has strongly opposed the proposal to divide Pakistan into multiple provinces. He cautioned that such a move could trigger violence and bloodshed in Karachi and Hyderabad. Reports have suggested that army chief Asim Munir is considering a plan to create 12 to 15 provinces.

Article Title: $135 billion in debt, still getting loans: Who is keeping Pakistan afloat, and why
Article Text:
Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and chief of defence forces Asim Munir (Reuters file photo)

What World Bank’s International Debt Report says about Pakistan

Pakistan’s economic challenges

China: Pakistan’s ‘all-weather’ friend

Why financial institutions continue lending to Pakistan

Can Pakistan actually repay its debt

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What happens if creditors stop lending to Pakistan

The World Bank ’s International Debt Report 2026 paints a stark picture of Pakistan’s growing external debt burden, showing that, as of 2025, Islamabad’s external debt had nearly doubled from its 2015 level.According to the report, Pakistan’s external debt stood at $135.1 billion last year, up from $68.7 billion in 2015, marking a 97% increase in just 10 years.Pakistan's mounting external debt presents a curious contradiction. Its economy continues to struggle, and its dependence on foreign financing remains substantial. Yet, despite these vulnerabilities, money continues to flow into the country from some of the world's most influential governments and financial institutions.The question, therefore, is not simply why Islamabad keeps borrowing, but why its creditors continue lending to a country whose ability to generate sufficient foreign exchange and meet its repayment obligations remains a source of concern.The $135.1 billion, which Pakistan owed as external debt, was up 4% from $129.9 billion in 2024. Of the 2025 debt, around $107.1 billion was public and publicly guaranteed debt, while the remainder included private-sector and short-term external obligations.Of Pakistan’s public and publicly guaranteed debt, nearly $57 billion is owed to multilateral creditors, while bilateral creditors account for over $42 billion, with the remainder owed to private creditors.Among individual creditors, China is Pakistan’s largest bilateral lender, accounting for $22.4 billion in debt. It is followed by the World Bank, with $19.2 billion, and the Asian Development Bank, with $16.83 billion, among other creditors.The report also highlighted the burden of debt repayments on Pakistan’s economy. In 2025, Islamabad spent an amount equivalent to 33% of its export earnings on servicing external debt, while total external debt stood at 34% of Gross National Income.The report, therefore, highlights the challenge facing Islamabad: managing its growing external debt while ensuring that its economy generates enough foreign exchange to meet repayment obligations.Continued lending does not necessarily mean Pakistan’s economy is healthy. Nor does its growing debt burden mean the country is on the verge of default.The latest economic indicators present a mixed picture.The World Bank estimates that Pakistan’s economy grew by 3.7% in FY26, up from 3.2% in the previous financial year. The fiscal deficit narrowed to 2.6% of GDP, while the current account recorded a small deficit of 0.1% of GDP. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) also reported that Pakistan’s gross foreign exchange reserves had risen to approximately $21.5 billion by the end of September 2025.These gains, however, are offset by continued economic challenges. Economic growth has not generated enough jobs for Pakistan’s growing workforce. About 3.5 million people enter the workforce every year, yet unemployment stood at 7% in 2024. While nearly 18 million new jobs have been created since 2018, most have been informal, low-paid or self-employment opportunities.Poverty, too, has increased, with the rate rising from 22% in 2018-19 to 29% in 2024-25. An estimated 70 million Pakistanis are now living in poverty.The future outlook also remains challenging. The World Bank projected Pakistan’s economy to grow by 3.8% in FY27, a marginal increase from the estimated 3.7% growth in FY26. Headline inflation was expected to rise to 8.2% in FY27 before easing to around 7%.The data therefore highlights the economic pressures Pakistan faces and is expected to confront in the coming years.China being Pakistan’s largest individual creditor is perhaps unsurprising. Beijing and Islamabad are, after all, each other’s “all-weather friends.”China’s investment in Pakistan has largely been channelled through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), the flagship project of Beijing’s ambitious Belt and Road Initiative. Under CPEC, Chinese investment in Pakistan is estimated at $62 billion over a period of 15 years.Another important feature of this economic relationship is loan rollover, under which a creditor extends the repayment period of existing loans instead of demanding immediate repayment. China has continued to roll over existing loans to Pakistan, providing Islamabad temporary relief from its foreign currency obligations without reducing its overall debt.With Pakistan struggling to repay its Chinese loans, what explains Beijing's willingness to not only continue providing financial support to Islamabad but also roll over existing loans?Sushant Sareen, senior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation and an expert on Pakistan, attributed Beijing's continued support to the “strategic relationship” between the two countries.“It’s not just about an economic relationship between them. I think one of the reasons why the Chinese keep bailing Pakistan out and give them money is because of the strategic relationship that exists between them,” Sareen told The Times of India.Even CPEC, he added, was China’s plan to “prop up” Pakistan’s economy and make it more efficient and productive.Ultimately, the question is whether Pakistan can generate enough foreign exchange to service its growing debt, even with continued support from China.That Beijing is Islamabad’s largest creditor comes as little surprise. However, multilateral institutions such as the IMF and the World Bank also continue to play an important role in financing Pakistan.Since joining the IMF in 1950, Pakistan has received around two dozen bailout packages. Most recently, in October, the IMF agreed to release another $1.21 billion under its ongoing loan and sustainability programmes, subject to Executive Board approval.In a recent YouTube interview, former IMF chief economist Gita Gopinath was asked why the lender continues to bail out Pakistan despite concerns over its ability to repay its loans.Gopinath explained that the IMF’s role is to help countries facing economic crises and that it cannot simply walk away from them.She also emphasised that the IMF's decisions are taken by its member countries, including India. The decision to extend a loan, therefore, rests with the membership rather than the IMF's management.Sareen echoed this view.“Pakistan is a member of the IMF. It is the IMF’s job to bail out countries which are facing balance of payments problems,” he said.He, however, pointed out that political considerations could also influence the IMF's lending decisions.“India holds slightly over 2% vote share and that's not big enough to veto the loan. The Americans with 16% or 17% stake can actually do that, because with 15% you can veto any IMF loan. And clearly the Americans don't want to turn the screws on the Pakistanis. So, yes, to some extent it is a political decision to give money to Pakistan,” he argued.Sareen noted, however, that overall, the IMF largely operates within its economic mandate.Taken together, Islamabad's repeated reliance on the IMF underlines the extent to which its economy depends on external financial support.Pakistan's total external debt of around $135 billion does not mean the entire amount is due for repayment immediately. The debt has accumulated over several years, with repayments spread across different periods.The extent of Pakistan's reliance on fresh borrowing is evident from the figures. In FY26, it received $16.16 billion in external loans, while repaying around $14.44 billion in external public debt, including $11.20 billion in principal and $3.24 billion in interest, according to the ministry of economic affairs.The key question, therefore, is whether Islamabad can generate enough foreign exchange to meet these repayment obligations while managing its other economic needs.Sareen argued that the bigger challenge for Pakistan was not repaying its entire debt, but servicing it — having enough foreign exchange to meet repayment and interest obligations as they fall due.“Pakistans' problem is that they're not earning the kind of foreign exchange they require to service that debt. And the debt which they're taking on is increasing virtually every year. But for now, they're managing to tide it over. They managed to avoid default, but at a very high price,” he said.The challenge for Islamabad, therefore, is not just to keep securing loans, but to build an economy capable of meeting its repayment obligations without repeatedly relying on external support.Pakistan is often described as a country facing economic collapse and the risk of disintegration. Its continued dependence on external financing raises an important question: what would happen if lenders stopped extending fresh loans to Islamabad?The withdrawal of support from its lenders would not automatically push Pakistan into default or close to disintegration. Rather, it would face severe economic difficulties.Sareen warned that a default could trigger severe economic hardship, with Pakistan potentially spending three to four years trying to stabilise its economy and regain access to the international financial system. During this period, it could struggle to maintain imports and deal with foreign exchange shortages.But Pakistan continues to stay afloat — with support from international institutions, as well as countries whose financial assistance is shaped by strategic interests. Lending decisions also have a political dimension, with the interests and influence of powerful member countries playing a role.For now, creditors continue to extend financial support, even as concerns over Islamabad's ability to repay its debt persist.
Article Summary: Pakistan's external debt stood at $135.1 billion last year, up from $68.7 billion in 2015. China is Pakistan’s largest bilateral lender, accounting for $22.4 billion in debt. Pakistan spent an amount equivalent to 33% of its export earnings on servicing external debt.

Article Title: 'Inevitable he will die in jail': Imran Khan's sons accuse Pak of torturing ex-PM
Article Text:
The interview comes as Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges through an open letter, seeking urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife

The sons of imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan have accused authorities of subjecting their father to prolonged physical and mental torture in Adiala Jail, warning that he could die in custody without urgent medical intervention.In an interview with Sky News's Mark Austin, Sulaiman Isa Khan and Kasim Khan expressed concern over the deteriorating health of the 74-year-old Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder, alleging that he was being kept in solitary confinement for 22 to 23 hours a day, with little human contact and no access to independent medical care."We can see the path that this is taking. It's inevitable that eventually he will die in this cell. He will be killed in this cell if he remains there any longer without proper treatment," the brothers said.They also alleged that prison authorities had instructed guards not to speak to their father, adding that the isolation was being used to exert psychological pressure on him."I mean, we've been saying this for months. They're torturing him in the cell. It's physical and mental torture. It's at a point where they've instructed the guards not to even speak to him while he's in the cell just to, you know, maintain pressure and mental pressure on him," they added.The brothers said authorities had failed to implement an August 18 Supreme Court order directing that Khan be shifted to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for medical examination and treatment. The order had also called for increased family access, including regular telephone conversations with his sons."Nothing's changed at all, despite an order from the Supreme Court back in August for him to be taken and treated at a private hospital called Shifa International, and for increased family access to his family, calls with us, regular calls with us. But none of that has been implemented. And his health has just continued to deteriorate," they said."His blood pressure is now dangerously high, at about 193, I think. So he needs to be treated at a private hospital immediately," they added.The interview comes as Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges through an open letter, seeking urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi. He said his blood pressure had risen sharply and doctors had warned of the risk of a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest.In the letter, released by his party and lawyer Salman Safdar, Khan also alleged that authorities had failed to implement the earlier hospital transfer order. "I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he said.However, Pakistan's cabinet minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed Khan's claims, saying he had received regular medical attention and had been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad eight times for examinations. The government has also rejected allegations of solitary confinement and denied that Khan was being denied access to his family.
Article Summary: Sulaiman Isa Khan and Kasim Khan accuse authorities of subjecting their father to prolonged physical and mental torture in Adiala Jail. They allege that he is being kept in solitary confinement for 22 to 23 hours a day, with little human contact and no access to independent medical care. Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges, seeking urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife.

Article Title: Former Pakistan army officer is new BLA chief
Article Text:
BLA appoints ex-Pakistan Army Captain as chief (file photo)

In a major organisational shift, Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has elevated its senior commander Rehman Gul to the post of commander-in-chief. Sources said his elevation carried symbolic weight given his past as a former captain in Pakistan army’s 19 Frontier Force (FF) Regiment.In 2010, Gul deserted the army, citing atrocities against civilians, and joined Aslam Baloch’s BLA, leaving the military brass flummoxed. Prior to assuming the top role, Gul served on the command council and led the Majeed Brigade, BLA’s operational wing which specialises in suicide bombings.Having graduated as a battalion senior major, Gul previously held military postings in Kotli in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir as well as North and South Waziristan, where he took part in military operations.The announcement also dispels earlier reports from the Pakistani military, which had declared Gul dead last year, a claim BLA didn’t validate. Adding a sensitive dynamic to the situation, sources indicate that Gul’s younger brother currently serves as a Major in the Pakistan army’s Signals Corps. Observers suggest that having a former military officer at the helm amplifies narratives of internal disillusionment among security personnel regarding state crackdowns and civilian casualties in Balochistan.The leadership transition, confirmed through a statement from group spokesperson Jeeyand Baloch on Nov 14, follows a unanimous vote by the outfit’s senior command council. The move comes just days after the announcement that Bashir Zeb was stepping down as chief.There was also uncertainty surrounding Zeb’s successor after the group said last week that Zeb was transferring all powers to the command council. While pro-Pak military social media accounts circulated rumours of Zeb having been poisoned by a confidante and being killed in Afghanistan, sources described them as false.
Article Summary: Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) elevate senior commander Rehman Gul to the post of commander-in-chief. Gul is a former captain in Pakistan army’s 19 Frontier Force (FF) Regiment. In 2010, Gul deserted the army, citing atrocities against civilians.

Article Title: Redrawing Pakistan: Ministers back 12-province plan but political, constitutional hurdles remain
Article Text:
Pakistan's 12-province proposal gains momentum as senior ministers back restructuring (Representative Image)

What the proposed 12-province map could look like

Political consensus remains the biggest hurdle

What the Constitution requires

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan's proposal to expand its four-province structure to as many as 12 has gathered momentum, with senior ministers backing it in the name of better governance. But the idea faces a major political hurdle: there is no consensus among the country's leading parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh.Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif has argued that Pakistan's growing population requires smaller provinces that can deliver public services more efficiently. Speaking to Geo News, he said the country could consider creating 12 provinces, provided the boundaries were drawn on administrative rather than linguistic, ethnic or political grounds.“If there is a proposal for 12 provinces, then make it 12,” Asif said, adding that new units should not be created to serve “language, ethnicity or political interests”.Pakistan’s interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has also revived the debate, suggesting a referendum to gauge public opinion on the contentious issue. His remarks have fuelled speculation that powerful quarters favour a broader restructuring of Pakistan's administrative map, with reports pointing to a possible constitutional exercise in 2027.No formal roadmap, however, has been announced. The proposed number of provinces, their boundaries and the process for creating them remain undecided.One proposal reported in Pakistani media envisages dividing Punjab into four provinces, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan into three each, and Sindh into two. The plan could involve a nationwide referendum and a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment, although neither has been confirmed as an approved government initiative.Supporters argue that the existing arrangement concentrates too much administrative and financial authority in provincial capitals leaving smaller cities and districts dependent on decisions taken far away.Asif has questioned whether federal funds transferred to provincial governments are reaching local institutions, arguing that decentralisation could bring decision-making and resources closer to communities. Advocates of the proposal say smaller provinces would make public services more accessible and help address uneven development.But the debate is not only about the size of administrative units. It also raises questions about whether creating more provinces would improve governance without stronger local governments and greater financial autonomy for districts.The proposal has exposed differences within the ruling coalition itself. The Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), led by Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, has firmly opposed any division of Sindh, while the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) has yet to settle on a formal position.The two parties are coalition partners in the federal government. The PML-N has said it will announce its position if the matter comes before Parliament, despite some of its leaders backing the creation of smaller provinces.A cabinet member in the Shehbaz Sharif government said reaching agreement would be difficult without the support of the major political parties.The issue has also prompted speculation about a possible understanding between the government and the main opposition, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI). PML-N leader and former federal minister Khawaja Saad Rafique has suggested that the establishment could offer relief to jailed former prime minister Imran Khan in return for PTI's support for the proposed constitutional changes. There has been no confirmation of such a deal.Smaller parties have also entered the debate. The Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) has renewed its demand for new administrative units in Sindh, while Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid chief Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain has called for new provinces to be considered through consultation and in the national interest.The Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party has backed the proposal on administrative grounds, while Jamaat-i-Islami has argued that the creation of new provinces should go hand in hand with strengthening local governments.Even if political parties agree on the broad idea, redrawing provincial boundaries would require a demanding constitutional process.Under Article 239 of Pakistan's Constitution, an amendment requires the support of at least two-thirds of the total membership of both houses of Parliament. If it changes the limits of an existing province, it must also secure the backing of at least two-thirds of the total membership of that province's assembly.That gives provincial parties considerable leverage over any proposed division.A nationwide referendum is not an automatic constitutional requirement for creating provinces. Any such exercise would need its own legal and constitutional basis, and Parliament could not simply be bypassed in deciding the process or framing the questions put to voters.Following a meeting between Pakistan’s president Asif Ali Zardari and prime minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday, a senior government official told news agency PTI that the two leaders had agreed to adhere strictly to the constitutional provisions governing the creation of new provinces. They also agreed that any proposed referendum would require parliamentary approval.Former federal information minister Muhammad Ali Durrani has meanwhile launched a campaign for the restoration of Bahawalpur province and the creation of 11 other smaller administrative units.For now, the proposal remains a subject of political debate rather than an agreed government plan. Any move to redraw the map would require agreement on boundaries, resources, parliamentary representation and the future of provincial institutions — as well as the constitutional numbers to make it happen.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif has argued that Pakistan's growing population requires smaller provinces that can deliver public services more efficiently. But the idea faces a major political hurdle: there is no consensus among the country's leading parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh.

Article Title: 24 militants, four soldiers killed in separate clashes in Pakistan's Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
(Photo credit: IANS)

At least 24 militants and four Pakistani soldiers, including an army officer, were killed in separate encounters between security forces and militants in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provinces, the Pakistan Army said on Saturday, PTI reported.The army said security forces had carried out multiple intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan since Friday, targeting militant hideouts in the areas of Kolpur, Kardagap and Nushki.During an operation in Kolpur on the intervening night of Friday and Saturday, troops killed eight militants, including a suicide bomber, and recovered a large cache of weapons and ammunition, the military said.The army said the militants used armed quadcopters to target military vehicles on patrol. The attack killed Major Omer Minhas Nasir and Havildar Muhammad Adnan Khan.Separately, security forces conducted operations against militant hideouts in Mir Ali, Datta Khel and surrounding areas of North Waziristan district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.According to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military's media wing, 16 militants were killed in the engagements. Twelve were killed in an operation in Ali Khel, while two each were killed in Mir Ali and Datta Khel.Two soldiers, Havildar Asmat Ali and Naik Aftab Ali, were killed during the operations. The ISPR said both soldiers fought bravely and laid down their lives in the line of duty. It added that the operations had dealt a major blow to the militant network.Weapons and ammunition were recovered from the slain militants, who, according to the military, were involved in several terrorist activities, including the killing of civilians.Pakistan's federal government uses the term 'Fitna al-Khawarij' for militants belonging to the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).
Article Summary: At least 24 militants and four Pakistani soldiers, including an army officer, were killed in separate encounters between security forces and militants. The Pakistan Army said security forces had carried out multiple intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan since Friday, targeting militant hideouts.

Article Title: 'Terrorist can return only in handcuffs': Bangladesh on Hasina's homecoming request
Article Text:
Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina

Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir on Tuesday ruled out an unconditional return for deposed former prime minister Sheikh Hasina , saying she could be brought back from India only "in handcuffs or under strict surveillance". The remarks came after reports that Hasina had sought to return to Bangladesh on December 16, the country's Victory Day."She can only be brought back in handcuffs or under strict surveillance," Kobir told reporters after briefing foreign diplomats on the situation in Bangladesh at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Dhaka, according to the state-run Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha (BSS).He was responding to a Reuters report that Hasina, who has been living in India since leaving Bangladesh in August 2024, wanted to return on Victory Day, which marks the country's independence from Pakistan in 1971."A distinction had to be drawn between what Hasina wanted and what could happen," Kobir said, according to BSS.According to The Daily Star, the minister also said, "The reality is that no terrorist will ever be allowed to return this way without extradition.""The people of Bangladesh see terrorism as coming from one source -- Awami terrorism, sponsored by Hasina from Delhi. Everyone knows this. It's not rocket science," he added.Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali had told Reuters that the former prime minister wanted the Bangladesh government to arrange her return from Delhi aboard the national carrier, Biman Bangladesh Airlines."Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5th, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," Ali told Reuters."Having exiled her contrary to the Constitution under such circumstances, it is now the responsibility of the government to make possible her return to Bangladesh on Victory Day on December 16th," he added.Kobir also addressed concerns over sporadic attacks in Bangladesh, alleging that Awami League supporters were behind incidents intended to frighten the public and accusing Hasina of sponsoring them. "(But) the attacks had failed to intimidate people," he said, according to The Daily Star.Asked how the government planned to handle the situation, Kobir said it was confident in its ability to respond. "We stand firmly with the people at all times. We're dealing with the situation confidently and taking our people into confidence," he said, as quoted by the newspaper.The briefing was attended by heads of diplomatic missions, United Nations agencies and international organisations, according to a note circulated by the foreign ministry.
Article Summary: Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir on Tuesday ruled out an unconditional return for deposed former prime minister Sheikh Hasina. Kobir said she could be brought back from India only "in handcuffs or under strict surveillance" The remarks came after reports that Hasina had sought to return to Bangladesh on December 16, the country's Victory Day.

Article Title: 5.4 magnitude earthquake jolts Nepal; tremors felt across parts of eastern India
Article Text:

A magnitude 5.4 earthquake struck Nepal’s Koshi Province early Tuesday morning, triggering tremors across parts of eastern and northeastern India, Bhutan and Bangladesh. Reports of shaking also emerged from parts of China, with residents in several areas experiencing the impact of the early-morning quake.The earthquake struck near Lelep in Nepal’s Koshi Province at around 7:02 am IST, according to initial reports from the United States Geological Survey (USGS). The National Centre for Seismology (NCS), meanwhile, recorded the tremor at magnitude 5.3, with its epicentre located at latitude 27.855°N and longitude 87.909°E, at a depth of 20 kilometres.Tremors were reported across parts of eastern and northeastern India, including Bihar, Meghalaya and North Bengal, as well as areas bordering the Himalayan region.Initial estimates from the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC), cited by Reuters, also placed the earthquake at magnitude 5.3, with a reported depth of around 10 kilometres.Separately, a magnitude 2.5 earthquake struck Assam’s Karbi Anglong district at 3:39 am on Tuesday. According to the NCS, the quake occurred at a depth of 15 kilometres, with its epicentre at latitude 25.743°N and longitude 93.355°E.Meanwhile, another earthquake was reported in Pakistan, near the Sindh-Balochistan border. The tremor was recorded at a depth of 17 kilometres, according to preliminary information.
Article Summary: A magnitude 5.4 earthquake struck Nepal’s Koshi Province early Tuesday morning, triggering tremors across parts of eastern and northeastern India, Bhutan and Bangladesh. Reports of shaking also emerged from parts of China, with residents in several areas experiencing the impact of the early-morning quake.
